Existing inference-time defenses either invalidate edits through conspicuous corruption, thereby exposing the protection, or allow them to proceed with identity or reference content drift, thereby failing to prevent the editing behavior itself. We instead target a stealthy and harmless no-op in which the requested edit is suppressed, the output remains natural and source-preserving without conspicuous artifacts or identity replacement, and harmful semantics requested by malicious instructions are absent. We propose NullEdit, which targets the VLM representation jointly formed from the reference image and instruction before it conditions the downstream DiT backbone. Using normal-edit and no-edit anchors, NullEdit redirects this representation, while cross-prompt gradient averaging transfers protection to held out instructions. Across Step1X-Edit and Qwen-Image-Edit on CelebA-HQ and VGGFace2, NullEdit reduces the EditReward IF score by 0.813 on average relative to the SOTA baseline while preserving subject identity and source content.

AI.tldr: NullEdit is an inference-time defense against unauthorized image editing that achieves a stealthy no-op effect by redirecting the joint vision-language model (VLM) representation formed from the reference image and instruction, suppressing unwanted edits while preserving naturalness and source content without conspicuous artifacts.
AI.motivation: Existing inference-time defenses against unauthorized image editing either corrupt edits visibly (exposing the protection) or allow edits with identity/content drift (failing to prevent the editing behavior). A stealthy defense that suppresses edits without artifacts while preserving source content is needed.
AI.method: NullEdit targets the VLM representation jointly formed from the reference image and instruction before it conditions the downstream DiT backbone. It uses normal-edit and no-edit anchors to redirect this representation, and employs cross-prompt gradient averaging to transfer protection to held-out instructions.
AI.result: Across Step1X-Edit and Qwen-Image-Edit on CelebA-HQ and VGGFace2, NullEdit reduces the EditReward IF score by 0.813 on average relative to the SOTA baseline while preserving subject identity and source content.
AI.conclusion: NullEdit provides an effective and stealthy defense that suppresses unauthorized edits by manipulating the VLM representation before it conditions the diffusion backbone, achieving significant reduction in edit effectiveness while maintaining image naturalness and identity preservation.

title: ConfTriage: A Calibration-Aware LLM Triage Framework for Pulmonary Nodule Malignancy with Selective Specialist Deferral
summary: Pulmonary nodule malignancy prediction typically depends on image-trained specialist deep learning (DL) models that require substantial annotated imaging data and task-specific training. We investigate whether a generalist large language model (LLM), reading only a faithful natural-language rendering of standard nodule attributes, can serve as a calibrated triage layer. We propose ConfTriage, a confidence-calibrated method built on three pillars: language as the modality, calibration as the safety mechanism, and a selective specialist DL backstop for low-confidence cases. We prove two guarantees: a finite-sample combined-error bound yielding an explicit per-threshold operational certificate, and an oracle inequality showing that excess risk over the Bayes-optimal deferral classifier is controlled by the L1 calibration error of the LLM probability. A controlled seven-way input ablation across five frontier LLMs on LIDC-IDRI shows that natural-language descriptions dominate the diagnostic signal, while low-level image statistics are essentially diagnostically vacuous. ConfTriage achieved an F1 score of 88.22% and an AUC of 0.92, resolving 76.5% of cases using zero-shot LLM inference alone and referring only uncertain cases to the specialist DL backstop. These results demonstrate that clinically meaningful diagnostic information can be captured through structured radiological descriptions and leveraged by calibrated LLMs for selective referral. The framework suggests a practical pathway for combining generalist LLM prediction with specialist AI models in medical decision-support systems. Source code is publicly available at https://github.com/rabiul-ai/ConfTriage.

AI.tldr: ConfTriage is a confidence-calibrated framework that uses generalist LLMs reading natural-language radiological descriptions to triage pulmonary nodule malignancy predictions, deferring low-confidence cases to specialist DL models, achieving F1=88.22%, AUC=0.92, and resolving 76.5% of cases via zero-shot LLM inference alone.
AI.motivation: Traditional DL-based pulmonary nodule malignancy prediction requires substantial annotated imaging data and task-specific training. The authors investigate whether generalist LLMs reading natural-language renderings of nodule attributes can serve as calibrated triage layers, potentially reducing reliance on large annotated imaging datasets while maintaining safety through calibration and selective referral.
AI.method: ConfTriage builds on three pillars: (1) language as the modality (natural-language rendering of nodule attributes), (2) calibration as the safety mechanism, and (3) a selective specialist DL backstop for low-confidence cases. The method proves two theoretical guarantees: a finite-sample combined-error bound providing per-threshold operational certificates, and an oracle inequality showing excess risk over the Bayes-optimal deferral classifier is controlled by L1 calibration error. A controlled seven-way input ablation was conducted across five frontier LLMs on LIDC-IDRI.
AI.result: Natural-language descriptions dominate the diagnostic signal while low-level image statistics are diagnostically vacuous. ConfTriage achieved F1=88.22%, AUC=0.92, resolving 76.5% of cases via zero-shot LLM inference alone, referring only uncertain cases to the specialist DL backstop.
AI.conclusion: Clinically meaningful diagnostic information can be captured through structured radiological descriptions and leveraged by calibrated LLMs for selective referral, suggesting a practical pathway for combining generalist LLM prediction with specialist AI models in medical decision-support systems.

title: GESTO: Human-Centric Spatio-Temporal Memory for Reasoning in Dynamic Scenes
summary: Robots operating in human environments need memories that capture not only what objects exist and where, but also how people use them over time and how individual interactions compose into goal-directed activities. Existing 4D scene graphs preserve object and place histories but omit activity structure, whereas activity representations are either not grounded in persistent 3D scenes or rely on externally provided event boundaries and object associations. We present GESTO (Grounded Event and Spatio-Temporal memOry), a spatio-temporal memory that couples a persistent 4D scene graph with a two-level hierarchy of atomic human--object interactions and goal-driven events. From an RGB-D observation stream, GESTO automatically extracts timestamped interactions, grounds them to persistent scene entities, groups them into events, and uses event context to refine uncertain object associations. A relation-aware tool-calling agent queries the resulting memory for activity-centric spatio-temporal reasoning. We evaluate GESTO on the reproducible text, binary, and time categories of an existing benchmark, together with 40 new Space2Event and Event2Space queries. GESTO achieves scores of 0.71, 0.75, and 0.70 on the standard categories, approaching a method supplied with ground-truth event and object grounding, while substantially outperforming the same reasoning framework when these inputs are removed. It further achieves 0.73 and 0.75 on Space2Event and Event2Space queries. Ablations show that hierarchical event structure and context-aware grounding refinement provide complementary benefits, supporting activity-grounded hierarchical memory for retrospective reasoning in dynamic human environments.

AI.tldr: GESTO is a spatio-temporal memory system that couples a persistent 4D scene graph with a two-level hierarchy of atomic human-object interactions and goal-driven events, enabling activity-centric spatio-temporal reasoning for robots in dynamic human environments.
AI.motivation: Existing 4D scene graphs capture object and place histories but lack activity structure, while activity representations are either not grounded in persistent 3D scenes or depend on externally provided event boundaries and object associations. Robots need memories that capture not only what objects exist and where, but also how people use them over time and how individual interactions compose into goal-directed activities.
AI.method: GESTO extracts timestamped human-object interactions from an RGB-D observation stream, grounds them to persistent scene entities, groups them into events in a two-level hierarchy (atomic interactions and goal-driven events), and uses event context to refine uncertain object associations. A relation-aware tool-calling agent queries the resulting memory for activity-centric spatio-temporal reasoning.
AI.result: On the standard text, binary, and time benchmark categories, GESTO achieves scores of 0.71, 0.75, and 0.70, approaching a method with ground-truth event and object grounding, while substantially outperforming the same reasoning framework without those inputs. It achieves 0.73 and 0.75 on the new Space2Event and Event2Space query categories.
AI.conclusion: Ablations show that hierarchical event structure and context-aware grounding refinement provide complementary benefits, supporting activity-grounded hierarchical memory for retrospective reasoning in dynamic human environments.

title: Sensor-Informed Per-Point Covariance for Structured-Light 3D Imaging
summary: Per-point uncertainty models are important in structured-light 3D reconstruction for probabilistic registration, fusion, and quality assessment. In practice, however, point-cloud covariances are often modeled as isotropic constants or inferred from local surface geometry and therefore do not explicitly reflect the measurement process. This is a limitation in fringe projection profilometry (FPP), where phase noise propagates through calibrated reconstruction and produces strongly anisotropic 3D uncertainty. This paper presents a sensor-informed first-order method for constructing a per-point 3 x 3 covariance field from experimentally measured phase precision and calibrated phase-to-depth and phase-to-3D mappings. The formulation separates a rank-1 phase-induced covariance from an effective full-rank completion obtained by incorporating fitted lateral image-space perturbation scales. Repeated-plane experiments under fixed imaging conditions show close alignment of the dominant covariance direction with the viewing ray, and consistency between the dominant phase-induced uncertainty scale and scalar depth uncertainty. In G-ICP registration, the proposed covariance substantially improves over a constant isotropic model while providing a sensor-derived uncertainty representation complementary to conventional geometry-based covariances.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a sensor-informed first-order method to construct per-point 3x3 covariance fields for fringe projection profilometry, derived from experimentally measured phase precision and calibrated mappings, which improves G-ICP registration over constant isotropic models.
AI.motivation: Existing point-cloud covariances in structured-light 3D reconstruction are often modeled as isotropic constants or inferred from local surface geometry, failing to reflect the actual measurement process. In fringe projection profilometry (FPP), phase noise propagates through calibrated reconstruction and produces strongly anisotropic 3D uncertainty, which is not captured by conventional models.
AI.method: The method constructs per-point 3x3 covariance fields using a sensor-informed first-order approach. It uses experimentally measured phase precision and calibrated phase-to-depth and phase-to-3D mappings. The formulation separates a rank-1 phase-induced covariance from an effective full-rank completion obtained by incorporating fitted lateral image-space perturbation scales.
AI.result: Repeated-plane experiments under fixed imaging conditions show close alignment of the dominant covariance direction with the viewing ray, and consistency between the dominant phase-induced uncertainty scale and scalar depth uncertainty. In G-ICP registration, the proposed covariance substantially improves over a constant isotropic model while providing a complementary uncertainty representation to conventional geometry-based covariances.
AI.conclusion: The proposed sensor-derived covariance provides a physically meaningful, anisotropic uncertainty representation that complements geometry-based approaches and significantly enhances probabilistic registration performance in fringe projection profilometry.

title: VIDS-Seg: Towards Reliable Uncertainty Quantification in Pediatric Cardiac Ultrasound Segmentation
summary: Reliable clinical deployment of machine learning requires models that know when they are likely to fail, particularly for subgroups underrepresented in training data. A common case is pediatric care, where models trained on adult cohorts can silently under-perform on children with no indication that something has gone wrong. As retraining with labeled pediatric data is often infeasible, detecting such failures at inference time is a critical clinical need. Building on the VIDS (Variational Inference under Distribution Shifts) framework, we introduce VIDS-Seg, which applies amortized variational inference over a lightweight prediction head to make this adaptive, OOD-aware prior tractable for dense image segmentation. We evaluate VIDS-Seg on left ventricular segmentation in echocardiography, a setting where pediatric anatomy differs systematically from the adult population most segmentation models are trained on, training on an adult cohort (EchoNet-Dynamic) and evaluating zero-shot on a pediatric cohort (EchoNet-Pediatric). Across all age strata, VIDS-Seg matches competitive baselines in segmentation accuracy while producing substantially higher spatial correspondence between predicted uncertainty and segmentation error, an advantage that persists even after applying temperature scaling to all baselines. Downstream, it yields more accurate and stable ejection fraction estimates and more reliable detection of cardiac malfunction in the infant subgroup. Our results indicate that OOD-aware uncertainty quantification can serve as a practical safety layer for deployed segmentation models, enabling detection of silent failures in underrepresented subgroups without retraining or additional labeled data.

AI.tldr: VIDS-Seg applies amortized variational inference under distribution shifts to provide OOD-aware uncertainty quantification for dense image segmentation, demonstrating practical utility in detecting silent failures when adult-trained LV segmentation models are applied zero-shot to pediatric echocardiography data.
AI.motivation: Machine learning models deployed in clinical settings can silently under-perform on underrepresented subgroups (e.g., pediatric patients when models are trained on adult cohorts). Retraining with labeled pediatric data is often infeasible, so detecting such failures at inference time is a critical clinical need.
AI.method: The authors extend the VIDS (Variational Inference under Distribution Shifts) framework to segmentation tasks (VIDS-Seg) by applying amortized variational inference over a lightweight prediction head, making adaptive, OOD-aware priors tractable for dense image segmentation.
AI.result: Trained on adult EchoNet-Dynamic and evaluated zero-shot on pediatric EchoNet-Pediatric, VIDS-Seg matches competitive baselines in segmentation accuracy across all age strata while producing substantially higher spatial correspondence between predicted uncertainty and segmentation error (even after temperature scaling). It also yields more accurate and stable ejection fraction estimates and more reliable detection of cardiac malfunction in the infant subgroup.
AI.conclusion: OOD-aware uncertainty quantification can serve as a practical safety layer for deployed segmentation models, enabling detection of silent failures in underrepresented subgroups without retraining or additional labeled data.

title: Order Matters: LVLMs as Judges for Temporal Reasoning in Image Sequences
summary: As generative multimedia evolves from static image synthesis to complex, interleaved visual narratives, a foundational bottleneck has emerged: the judgment crisis. While human perception naturally synthesizes the temporal and logical flow of a story, automated evaluation systems remain largely "blind" to sequential continuity, often failing to distinguish between a coherent narrative and a semantically shuffled or contradictory sequence. This work identifies a critical structural gap in current multimodal evaluation paradigms, arguing that the reliance on Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) as judges is fundamentally limited by architectural biases. Our analysis reveals a profound performance dichotomy: while models may appear competent in isolated pointwise scoring, they suffer a catastrophic collapse when required to perform pairwise discrimination of temporal order. We demonstrate that this is not merely a data-scarcity issue but a structural one. Through a series of diagnostic probes, we uncover systematic positional asymmetries, specifically primacy and recency effects, where a model's judgment of a story is significantly influenced by the placement of a frame, often more than by its semantic consistency. These biases, potentially rooted in causal masking and rotary embeddings, suggest that current transformer-based judges are inherently ill-equipped for long-form visual reasoning. By exposing these blind spots, we challenge the multimedia community to move beyond snapshot-centric metrics and instead pioneer Temporally-Aware Evaluation paradigms that treat visual sequences as unified logical structures rather than unordered collections of frames.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a fundamental "judgment crisis" in multimodal evaluation: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) used as judges fail to assess temporal/sequential continuity in visual narratives. Through diagnostic probes, the authors reveal that LVLMs suffer from catastrophic performance collapse in pairwise temporal-order discrimination, exhibiting systematic positional biases (primacy and recency effects) potentially rooted in architectural features like causal masking and rotary embeddings. The work argues this is a structural problem, not a data-scarcity issue, and calls for a shift toward Temporally-Aware Evaluation paradigms.
AI.motivation: Current automated evaluation systems are "blind" to sequential continuity in interleaved visual narratives, failing to distinguish coherent stories from semantically shuffled or contradictory sequences. The authors aim to expose this structural gap in multimodal evaluation, showing that LVLMs as judges are fundamentally limited by architectural biases rather than just data scarcity.
AI.method: The paper conducts a series of diagnostic probes on LVLMs to assess temporal-order discrimination, revealing a dichotomy between pointwise scoring competence and pairwise discrimination collapse. They analyze positional asymmetries (primacy and recency effects) to trace systematic biases to architectural components such as causal masking and rotary embeddings.
AI.result: LVLMs exhibit catastrophic performance collapse on pairwise temporal-order discrimination despite appearing competent on isolated pointwise scoring. Systematic positional asymmetries are uncovered, where frame placement influences judgment more than semantic consistency. These biases are traced to architectural features including causal masking and rotary position embeddings.
AI.conclusion: The judgment crisis in multimodal evaluation is a structural problem inherent to transformer-based architectures, not merely a data issue. The authors call on the multimedia community to move beyond snapshot-centric metrics and develop Temporally-Aware Evaluation paradigms that treat visual sequences as unified logical structures rather than unordered collections of frames.

title: Temporally Grounded Compositional Camera Motion Understanding via Geometric Knowledge Distillation
summary: Understanding camera motion is fundamental to video perception, with applications in spatial intelligence and controllable video generation. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a natural interface for this task, but existing work typically assigns one or more labels to an entire clip. Such clip-level recognition overlooks two defining properties of real camera motion: it can change within a shot, and multiple movements can occur simultaneously. We therefore formulate camera-motion understanding as temporally grounded, compositional recognition, which requires a model to localize motion-consistent intervals and identify every movement active within each interval. We introduce CamChoreo, a benchmark of 4,229 real single-shot clips with expert-annotated temporal segments. Its annotations use a compact vocabulary of 20 direction-aware labels, and nearly half of the segments contain compound camera motion, with multiple movement primitives active simultaneously. Recognizing such fine-grained, compositional motion is hard for current MLLMs, whose visual encoders emphasize semantic content rather than the geometric evidence on which camera motion depends. Directly injecting features from a frozen 3D foundation model addresses this gap, but requires running the expensive geometry model on every input; we refer to this baseline as CamInject. We instead propose CamDistill, which distills the same geometric knowledge into lightweight camera tokens during training and removes the 3D model at inference. CamDistill matches the accuracy of direct feature injection without running the 3D teacher at inference. Together, CamChoreo and CamDistill advance camera-motion understanding from clip-level labeling to temporally grounded, compositional recognition. Project page: https://ddz16.github.io/cammotion.github.io/.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CamChoreo, a benchmark of 4,229 real single-shot clips with expert-annotated temporal segments for camera-motion understanding, formulated as temporally grounded compositional recognition. It also proposes CamDistill, a method that distills geometric knowledge from a frozen 3D foundation model into lightweight camera tokens, matching the accuracy of direct feature injection (CamInject) without running the expensive 3D model at inference.
AI.motivation: Existing camera-motion recognition assigns clip-level labels, overlooking that camera motion can change within a shot and multiple movements can occur simultaneously. This motivates reformulating camera-motion understanding as temporally grounded, compositional recognition to capture these properties.
AI.method: The paper builds CamChoreo, a benchmark with 4,229 single-shot clips annotated with temporally grounded segments using a 20-label vocabulary, where nearly half contain compound motion. It proposes CamDistill, which distills geometric knowledge from a frozen 3D foundation model into lightweight camera tokens during training, removing the 3D model at inference—contrasting with CamInject, which injects features from the 3D model directly on every input.
AI.result: CamDistill matches the accuracy of direct feature injection (CamInject) without requiring the expensive 3D model at inference time, demonstrating that geometric knowledge can be effectively distilled into lightweight tokens.
AI.conclusion: Together, CamChoreo and CamDistill advance camera-motion understanding from clip-level labeling to temporally grounded, compositional recognition, addressing the limitations of prior approaches while maintaining inference efficiency.

title: SafeCA: Safe Cross-Attention Localization and Regulation for Text-to-Video Jailbreak Defense
summary: Text-to-Video (T2V) generative models are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks in real-world deployment, leading them to produce harmful or inappropriate content. Existing defense approaches mainly rely on input filtering or reconstruction, which not only incur high computational latency but also tend to distort semantics. To address these issues, we experimentally and systematically analyze the differences between clean and jailbreak samples in the cross-attention feature space, revealing for the first time a cumulative separation effect and a progressively increasing trend of linear separability between the two during the diffusion process. Based on this insight, we propose SafeCA, a feature-level defense mechanism for safe cross-attention localization and regularization. Firstly, we identify key defensive regions and values through attention stability analysis using cross-attention features collected from clean prompts within a single inference. Secondly, SafeCA mitigates anomalous activations via attention masking with energy normalization and introduces a lightweight semantic-space adapter to redirect abnormal semantic flows. Furthermore, we detect and suppress potentially malicious tokens by back-propagating feature anomaly signals to the input cue words, thereby enhancing the deployability of the defense in commercial models. Experimental results show that SafeCA reduces the jailbreak success rate by about 20% on mainstream T2V models, adds almost no inference overhead (+0.1s), and maintains good text-video semantic consistency. Overall, SafeCA provides an architecture-level, deployable protection paradigm for T2V generation models.

AI.tldr: SafeCA is a feature-level defense mechanism for Text-to-Video (T2V) models that mitigates jailbreak attacks by analyzing cumulative separation effects in cross-attention feature space, using attention masking, energy normalization, and a semantic-space adapter to suppress malicious tokens while adding negligible inference overhead (+0.1s) and reducing jailbreak success rate by ~20%.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses for T2V jailbreak attacks rely on input filtering or reconstruction, which suffer from high computational latency and semantic distortion. There is a need for a more efficient and less intrusive defense approach that operates at the feature level rather than the input level.
AI.method: SafeCA works in three steps: (1) identifying key defensive regions and values through attention stability analysis using cross-attention features from clean prompts within a single inference; (2) mitigating anomalous activations via attention masking with energy normalization and introducing a lightweight semantic-space adapter to redirect abnormal semantic flows; (3) detecting and suppressing malicious tokens by back-propagating feature anomaly signals to input cue words.
AI.result: SafeCA reduces jailbreak success rate by approximately 20% on mainstream T2V models, adds almost no inference overhead (+0.1s), and maintains good text-video semantic consistency.
AI.conclusion: SafeCA provides an architecture-level, deployable protection paradigm for T2V generation models, leveraging cross-attention feature analysis to achieve effective and efficient jailbreak defense without significant computational cost or semantic degradation.

title: GS-CPE: Unified 6-Degree-of-Freedom Camera Pose Estimation via 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Despite substantial progress in visual localization, from scene coordinate regression to direct camera pose regression, achieving both robust generalization and high accuracy remain challenging. This study introduces GS-CPE (Gaussian Splatting based Camera Pose Estimation), a coarse-to-fine framework for 6-DoF camera pose estimation that unifies geometry-based coarse pose estimation with robust 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) warping based pose refinement. GS-CPE first estimates a coarse pose via retrieval-guided geometric pose estimation on a 3DGS scene representation, then refines it by minimizing a visibility aware masked RGB warping objective in a multi-scale optimization framework, with adaptive re-rendering. Extensive experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks including 7Scenes, Cambridge Landmarks, FAST-LIVO2 datasets, and a custom dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming in both accuracy and generalization.

AI.tldr: GS-CPE is a coarse-to-fine 6-DoF camera pose estimation framework that combines geometric coarse pose estimation with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) warping-based refinement, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and generalization across indoor and outdoor benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing visual localization methods (scene coordinate regression and direct camera pose regression) struggle to achieve both robust generalization and high accuracy simultaneously. A unified approach is needed to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: GS-CPE uses a two-stage pipeline: (1) coarse pose estimation via retrieval-guided geometric pose estimation on a 3DGS scene representation, and (2) pose refinement by minimizing a visibility-aware masked RGB warping objective within a multi-scale optimization framework featuring adaptive re-rendering.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 7Scenes, Cambridge Landmarks, FAST-LIVO2 datasets, and a custom dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming existing methods in both accuracy and generalization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed coarse-to-fine GS-CPE framework successfully unifies geometry-based coarse estimation with robust 3DGS warping-based refinement, showing that this combination yields superior accuracy and generalization for 6-DoF camera pose estimation.

title: Mixture-of-Experts-based Entropy Model for Learned Image Compression
summary: Learned image compression has seen significant progress in recent years with the development of end-to-end learned models that achieve better compression efficiency than state-of-the-art conventional methods. Recently, Mixture of Experts (MoE) approaches have seen promising results in NLP and computer vision tasks. In this paper, we introduce the MoE approach to learned image compression. We propose a MoE-based Entropy model (MoEE) for learned image compression, allowing the model to selectively activate only the subset of parameters required for the input image. Our model achieves a BD-Rate improvement over VVC of -16.85% on the Kodak dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Mixture of Experts (MoE) based entropy model (MoEE) for learned image compression, which selectively activates only necessary parameters for each input image, achieving a BD-Rate improvement of -16.85% over VVC on the Kodak dataset.
AI.motivation: Learned image compression has advanced significantly, but existing models typically use all parameters for every input regardless of the image's specific characteristics. MoE approaches have shown promise in NLP and vision tasks by selectively routing inputs to specialized experts, motivating the authors to bring this efficient parameter specialization to learned image compression.
AI.method: The authors propose a Mixture of Experts based Entropy model (MoEE) for learned image compression. The model routes each input image through a subset of expert parameters, selectively activating only the parameters needed for that particular input, rather than using the entire parameter set for every image.
AI.result: The proposed MoEE model achieves a BD-Rate improvement of -16.85% over VVC on the Kodak dataset, demonstrating superior compression efficiency compared to the state-of-the-art conventional codec.
AI.conclusion: Introducing MoE to learned image compression is effective, as selectively activating only relevant parameters per input improves compression efficiency beyond conventional standards like VVC.

title: StreamFlow: Dynamic Memory Flows for Streaming Video Understanding
summary: Streaming video understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to preserve relevant evidence from continuously evolving streams under strict causality and bounded memory. Yet existing paradigms remain limited: model-based methods require intrusive backbone updates, while memory-based methods expend substantial visual-encoding computation on temporally redundant content and rely on rigid access to visual history. To address these limitations, we introduce StreamFlow, an efficient visual memory framework that enables dynamic, on-demand access to historical visual information. StreamFlow combines a lightweight, dynamics-aware mid-term memory that filters temporal redundancy before visual encoding with a latent long-term memory that consolidates historical video content into visual latents accessible to subsequent reasoning. During generation, an attention-guided retrieval mechanism injects relevant visual latents when the model's reliance on visual evidence weakens. StreamFlow achieves state-of-the-art streaming video understanding performance, reaching 67.73% overall accuracy on StreamingBench, while also delivering strong performance on offline long-video benchmarks. Relative to the vanilla setting, it improves the visual attention score (VAS) by 59.1% while reducing end-to-end latency and peak memory by 50.4% and 21.1%, respectively, enabling more visually grounded and efficient reasoning.

AI.tldr: StreamFlow is an efficient visual memory framework for streaming video understanding that combines a lightweight dynamics-aware mid-term memory to filter temporal redundancy before visual encoding with a latent long-term memory that consolidates historical content into visual latents. An attention-guided retrieval mechanism injects relevant visual latents during generation when the model's reliance on visual evidence weakens. It achieves 67.73% overall accuracy on StreamingBench, improves VAS by 59.1% while reducing latency and peak memory by 50.4% and 21.1% respectively.
AI.motivation: Existing streaming video understanding paradigms are limited: model-based methods require intrusive backbone updates, while memory-based methods waste visual-encoding computation on temporally redundant content and rely on rigid access to visual history. There is a need for dynamic, on-demand access to historical visual information under strict causality and bounded memory constraints.
AI.method: StreamFlow combines two memory components: (1) a lightweight dynamics-aware mid-term memory that filters temporal redundancy before visual encoding, and (2) a latent long-term memory that consolidates historical video content into visual latents accessible to subsequent reasoning. During generation, an attention-guided retrieval mechanism injects relevant visual latents when the model's reliance on visual evidence weakens.
AI.result: StreamFlow achieves state-of-the-art streaming video understanding with 67.73% overall accuracy on StreamingBench, along with strong performance on offline long-video benchmarks. It improves the visual attention score (VAS) by 59.1% and reduces end-to-end latency and peak memory by 50.4% and 21.1% respectively, relative to the vanilla setting.
AI.conclusion: StreamFlow enables more visually grounded and efficient reasoning for streaming video understanding by providing dynamic, on-demand access to historical visual information without requiring intrusive backbone modifications or wasting computation on redundant content.

title: Multiple Scale Latents for Learned Image Compression
summary: Most learned image compression systems rely on a single latent representation combined with a hyperprior, which limits their ability to efficiently capture image structure across spatial scales. In this work, we propose a hierarchical latent representation to improve the efficiency of the entropy model. By using multiple latents at different scales, each with its own entropy model, we better capture the spatial structure of the latent representation. Our experiments show that this approach achieves a 17.9% BD-rate reduction over VVC on Kodak, demonstrating the effectiveness of multi-scale latent representations. Furthermore, the approach is orthogonal to other advances in learned image compression, making it a versatile addition to existing methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hierarchical (multi-scale) latent representation for learned image compression, where multiple latents at different scales each have their own entropy model to better capture spatial structure. It achieves a 17.9% BD-rate reduction over VVC on Kodak and is orthogonal to other advances in learned image compression.
AI.motivation: Most learned image compression systems use a single latent representation with a hyperprior, which limits their ability to efficiently capture image structure across spatial scales.
AI.method: The authors propose a hierarchical latent representation with multiple latents at different scales, each having its own entropy model, to better capture the spatial structure of the latent representation.
AI.result: The approach achieves a 17.9% BD-rate reduction over VVC on Kodak, demonstrating the effectiveness of multi-scale latent representations.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical latent representation is effective for image compression and is orthogonal to other advances in learned image compression, making it a versatile addition to existing methods.

title: Evidence-Grounded Trustworthy Multimodal Reasoning and Evaluation Benchmark in Complex Urban Scenes
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate impressive performance in benign scenarios, their cognitive reliability deteriorates significantly in complex scenes under adverse conditions. In these settings, models often rely on implicit inference without sufficient visual evidence, leading to a disconnect between perception and reasoning. Meanwhile, existing outcome-oriented benchmarks evaluate only final predictions and fail to diagnose failures in the underlying reasoning process. To address this gap, the authors propose AD2-Bench, which introduces a Hierarchical Visual Diagnosis framework that decomposes reasoning into a structured Chain of Evidence (CoE). This fine-grained diagnosis reveals that robust multimodal reasoning fundamentally depends on accurate evidence acquisition. Building on this perspective, the authors formulate reasoning from a probabilistic viewpoint and identify two primary causes of reasoning failure: Spatial Ambiguity, where models fail to distinguish target objects from background clutter, resulting in localization errors; and Semantic Uncertainty, where degraded visual features lead to incorrect semantic interpretation, resulting in understanding errors. To overcome these evidence deficiencies, they further propose Evidence-grounded Visual Reasoning (EGVOR), which replaces implicit reasoning with the explicit generation of Evidence Atoms - structured spatial-semantic triplets that enforce tight alignment between localization and semantic understanding. The model is trained through a hierarchical curriculum that progresses from reflective supervision construction to reinforcement learning, where reducing reasoning variance is explicitly rewarded. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EGVOR substantially improves reasoning stability under adverse conditions, providing a more robust framework for trustworthy multimodal cognition.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AD2-Bench, a benchmark with a Hierarchical Visual Diagnosis framework that decomposes multimodal reasoning into a Chain of Evidence to diagnose reasoning failures in adverse conditions. It identifies two failure causes (Spatial Ambiguity and Semantic Uncertainty) and introduces EGVOR, a method using explicit Evidence Atoms (spatial-semantic triplets) trained via a hierarchical curriculum with reinforcement learning to improve reasoning stability.
AI.motivation: MLLMs perform well in benign scenarios but degrade in complex, adverse conditions where they rely on implicit inference without sufficient visual evidence, causing a disconnect between perception and reasoning. Existing outcome-oriented benchmarks only evaluate final predictions and fail to diagnose failures in the underlying reasoning process.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) AD2-Bench with a Hierarchical Visual Diagnosis framework that decomposes reasoning into a structured Chain of Evidence (CoE); (2) a probabilistic formulation identifying two failure causes - Spatial Ambiguity and Semantic Uncertainty; (3) EGVOR, which replaces implicit reasoning with explicit generation of Evidence Atoms (structured spatial-semantic triplets); (4) training via a hierarchical curriculum progressing from reflective supervision construction to reinforcement learning that rewards reducing reasoning variance.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show EGVOR substantially improves reasoning stability under adverse conditions, providing a more robust framework for trustworthy multimodal cognition.
AI.conclusion: Robust multimodal reasoning fundamentally depends on accurate evidence acquisition; explicit, evidence-grounded reasoning frameworks outperform implicit reasoning approaches in adverse conditions, leading to more trustworthy multimodal cognition.

title: Once Poisoned, Arbitrarily Controlled: A Programmable Backdoor in VLMs
summary: Existing vision-language model (VLM) backdoors are usually treated as static vulnerabilities: one-to-one and N-to-N attacks bind one or more triggers to a finite set of targets before victim training. This assumption substantially underestimates the threat. We show that a single poisoning phase can implant a programmable backdoor into a VLM, allowing an attacker to choose previously unseen target-caption semantics at inference time and synthesize corresponding stealthy triggers on demand. Unlike fixed-mapping attacks, the proposed any-to-any caption-control paradigm decouples post-training target selection from poisoning, enabling dynamic control of target captions without retraining the VLM. Our method has two components. First, a heuristic poisoning strategy exposes the model to diverse trigger-caption pairs, encouraging it to learn a general trigger-as-instruction rule rather than memorize a specific backdoor pattern. Second, a feature-space trigger steganography method maps any attacker-specified target caption to a stealthy visual trigger, implemented as either a norm-controlled perturbation or a non-semantic patch. Once inserted into arbitrary images, these triggers cause the poisoned VLM to generate outputs semantically aligned with the chosen target caption, even when the target was unseen during poisoning. Extensive experiments show that our attack achieves high any-to-any caption-control success rates, preserves clean model utility, and remains effective under several classical backdoor defenses.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a programmable backdoor attack for vision-language models (VLMs) that enables any-to-any caption control. Unlike static backdoors with fixed trigger-target mappings, a single poisoning phase allows attackers to choose previously unseen target captions at inference time and generate corresponding stealthy triggers on demand, without retraining the model.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM backdoors are treated as static vulnerabilities with one-to-one or N-to-N trigger-target bindings established before training. This underestimates the threat model—real attackers may want flexible, dynamic control over outputs, choosing targets post-training without access to the victim model.
AI.method: The method has two components: (1) a heuristic poisoning strategy that exposes the model to diverse trigger-caption pairs, teaching a general "trigger-as-instruction" rule rather than fixed pattern memorization, and (2) a feature-space trigger steganography method that maps any attacker-specified target caption to a stealthy visual trigger, implemented as either a norm-controlled perturbation or a non-semantic patch.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate high any-to-any caption-control success rates, preserved clean model utility, and effectiveness against several classical backdoor defenses.
AI.conclusion: The proposed programmable backdoor significantly elevates the threat landscape for VLMs by decoupling post-training target selection from poisoning, enabling dynamic attacker control over caption generation without model retraining.

title: CARE: Confidence-Aware Reasoning for Reliable Medical VQA
summary: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) has enabled medical Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to produce Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning for visual question answering, yet these models suffer from $\textit{confidence miscalibration}$---a systematic gap between expressed certainty and actual diagnostic accuracy that undermines clinical trust. We propose $\textbf{CARE}$, a $\textbf{C}$onfidence-$\textbf{A}$ware medical $\textbf{RE}$asoning framework that jointly optimizes accuracy and calibration through a dual-stage pipeline. First, a scalable Medical-CoT synthesis provides structured cold-start data for Supervised Fine-Tuning. Second, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a novel $\textbf{Confidence-Aware Reward (CAR)}$ mechanism ties the model's confidence to diagnostic correctness within the reward signal. Across three Medical VQA benchmarks, $\textbf{CARE}$ achieves the highest diagnostic accuracy while obtaining the lowest Expected Calibration Error and Hallucination Rate, establishing a foundation for trustworthy clinical decision support. Our code is available at https://github.com/anotherbricki/CARE.

AI.tldr: CARE is a confidence-aware medical reasoning framework that jointly optimizes accuracy and calibration for Medical MLLMs by combining supervised fine-tuning on synthesized Medical-CoT data with Group Relative Policy Optimization using a novel Confidence-Aware Reward mechanism, achieving the best diagnostic accuracy with the lowest calibration error and hallucination rate across three Medical VQA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning enables medical MLLMs to generate CoT reasoning for visual question answering, but these models suffer from confidence miscalibration—a systematic gap between expressed certainty and actual diagnostic accuracy—which undermines clinical trust.
AI.method: CARE uses a dual-stage pipeline: (1) a scalable Medical-CoT synthesis generates structured cold-start data for Supervised Fine-Tuning; (2) GRPO with a novel Confidence-Aware Reward (CAR) mechanism incorporates the model's confidence and its alignment with diagnostic correctness directly into the reward signal.
AI.result: Across three Medical VQA benchmarks, CARE achieves the highest diagnostic accuracy while obtaining the lowest Expected Calibration Error and Hallucination Rate.
AI.conclusion: CARE establishes a foundation for trustworthy clinical decision support by demonstrating that jointly optimizing accuracy and calibration in medical MLLMs is feasible and effective, with code released publicly.

title: A Dataset and Benchmark for Optical Music Recognition of String Quartet Scores
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the ISMIR 2026
summary: Optical music recognition (OMR) transcribes music scores into digital formats. While the field has advanced significantly on monophonic and piano-form scores, multi-part score transcription remains underexplored, largely due to the absence of a suitable dataset. We introduce OpenScore String Quartet for Optical Music Recognition (OSSQ-OMR), the first dataset dedicated to multi-part OMR. Built on the OpenScore String Quartet corpus, OSSQ-OMR pairs digitally encoded scores with their original scanned editions from IMSLP, with all images visually aligned to their transcriptions. The dataset is released with score images at system and staff levels, and paired transcriptions in three encoding formats: Extended Linearized MusicXML (LMXE), **kern, and ABC. In total, OSSQ-OMR contains 24,544 system images and 98,172 staff images drawn from 116 string quartet scores. We accompany the dataset with a benchmark protocol and baseline results from two representative OMR models, evaluated across four random score-level splits with mutually exclusive test sets. Baselines reach OMR-NED as low as 3.6% on synthetic and 5.9% on scanned inputs; results reveal substantial effects of encoding and segmentation choices, with the LSTM-based baseline degrading on scanned inputs roughly 2.6 times less than the Transformer-based baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OSSQ-OMR, the first dataset dedicated to multi-part optical music recognition, containing 24,544 system images and 98,172 staff images from 116 string quartet scores with paired transcriptions in three encoding formats. The authors provide a benchmark protocol and baseline results from two OMR models, showing OMR-NED as low as 3.6% on synthetic and 5.9% on scanned inputs.
AI.motivation: Multi-part score transcription remains underexplored in OMR largely due to the absence of a suitable dataset, despite significant advances on monophonic and piano-form scores. This paper aims to fill this gap by providing the first dedicated multi-part OMR dataset.
AI.method: The authors built OSSQ-OMR on the OpenScore String Quartet corpus, pairing digitally encoded scores with their original scanned editions from IMSLP, with all images visually aligned to their transcriptions. The dataset provides score images at system and staff levels, paired with transcriptions in Extended Linearized MusicXML (LMXE), **kern, and ABC formats. They establish a benchmark protocol with four random score-level splits and evaluate two representative OMR models.
AI.result: Baselines reach OMR-NED as low as 3.6% on synthetic and 5.9% on scanned inputs. Results reveal substantial effects of encoding and segmentation choices, with the LSTM-based baseline degrading on scanned inputs roughly 2.6 times less than the Transformer-based baseline.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and benchmark protocol establish a foundation for multi-part OMR research, highlighting the significant impact of encoding and segmentation choices on model performance, and demonstrating that different model architectures exhibit varying robustness to scanned (vs. synthetic) inputs.

title: ThinkAfford: Affordance-Centric Reasoning for Fine-Grained 3D Grounding in Cluttered Scenes
summary: Task-driven 3D affordance grounding aims to localize the functional region in a cluttered 3D scene that enables an action specified by a natural-language instruction. Existing methods either predict 3D masks directly or construct them by selecting and fusing intermediate 2D/3D regions. However, they remain vulnerable to two intertwined failure modes: the predicted or selected regions may miss the target interaction area or have unsuitable granularity, while language grounding may confuse visually similar alternatives under relational instructions. To this end, we introduce ThinkAfford, which decouples high-recall affordance proposal generation from instruction-grounded reasoning. Specifically, the Affordance Proposal Generation module first uses learnable affordance prompts and multi-level visual features to predict interaction-conditioned heatmaps, extracting a variable number of fine-grained proposals without parsed object or part names as segmentation prompts. Visual-Prompted Affordance Reasoning then reasons over labeled proposal overlays using the full instruction, returning identifiers in a structured "think-then-answer" response. Moreover, Group Relative Policy Optimization uses proposal-level rewards from lifted 3D overlap to align VPAR selection with final 3D grounding. On the SceneFun3D validation split, ThinkAfford achieves 10.69% AP50 and 25.46% AP25 under the official evaluator, outperforming comparable 3D open-vocabulary and vision-language-model-based 2D-to-3D baselines. Module-level diagnostics further show that APG attains 77.5% recall at 25% intersection-over-union, while GRPO-trained VPAR achieves 72.1% selection accuracy on APG-covered queries, compared with 63.4% under supervised fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: ThinkAfford decouples high-recall affordance proposal generation from instruction-grounded reasoning for task-driven 3D affordance grounding, using learnable affordance prompts for heatmap-based proposal generation, visual-prompted reasoning with structured "think-then-answer" responses, and Group Relative Policy Optimization to align proposal selection with final 3D grounding. It achieves 10.69% AP50 and 25.46% AP25 on SceneFun3D, outperforming comparable baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D affordance grounding methods suffer from two intertwined failure modes: (1) predicted or selected regions may miss the target interaction area or have unsuitable granularity, and (2) language grounding may confuse visually similar alternatives under relational instructions.
AI.method: ThinkAfford consists of two decoupled modules: (1) Affordance Proposal Generation (APG) uses learnable affordance prompts and multi-level visual features to predict interaction-conditioned heatmaps, extracting variable numbers of fine-grained proposals without needing parsed object/part names; (2) Visual-Prompted Affordance Reasoning (VPAR) reasons over labeled proposal overlays using the full instruction, returning identifiers in a structured "think-then-answer" response. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses proposal-level rewards from lifted 3D overlap to align VPAR selection with final 3D grounding.
AI.result: ThinkAfford achieves 10.69% AP50 and 25.46% AP25 on the SceneFun3D validation split under the official evaluator, outperforming 3D open-vocabulary and vision-language-model-based 2D-to-3D baselines. APG attains 77.5% recall at 25% IoU, and GRPO-trained VPAR achieves 72.1% selection accuracy on APG-covered queries versus 63.4% under supervised fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling proposal generation from instruction-grounded reasoning, combined with GRPO-based alignment using 3D overlap rewards, effectively improves 3D affordance grounding accuracy and robustness over existing baselines.

title: PEAK: Precise and Persistent Concept Erasure via k-Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Erasing concepts from large-scale text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models has become increasingly crucial due to the growing concerns over copyright infringement, privacy violations, and offensive content. Existing approaches struggle to achieve both precise and persistent concept erasure: inaccurate localization of concept-related representations may cause unintended semantic interference, while incomplete removal of the underlying concept knowledge allows adversarial recovery. To address this dilemma, we propose PEAK, a \textbf{\textit{precise}} and \textbf{\textit{persistent}} concept erasure framework via k-Sparse Autoencoders (kSAEs). PEAK first trains a kSAE on internal activations of the diffusion denoising network to decompose dense representations into interpretable sparse features. By contrasting sparse activations induced by target and non-target prompts, PEAK identifies a compact set of target-specific features according to both activation strength and frequency. These localized features are then used for parameter optimization, where PEAK selectively suppresses target-related activations while preserving complementary non-target ones towards the original model. This feature-guided optimization embeds concept erasure directly into diffusion parameters, eliminating the need for additional inference-time intervention and facilitating effective persistence against adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PEAK achieves effective and robust concept erasure. On the I2P benchmark, PEAK reduces NudeNet detections from 582 to 6, lowers the average attack success rate (ASR) from 96.52\% to 5.63\%, and preserves general generation quality on MS-COCO with a near-zero KID. Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/manmanTAT/PEAK

AI.tldr: PEAK is a concept erasure framework for text-to-image diffusion models that uses k-Sparse Autoencoders (kSAEs) to decompose dense internal representations into interpretable sparse features, precisely identify target-specific features via contrasting activations, and embed erasure directly into model parameters for persistent removal against adversarial attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing concept erasure methods for T2I diffusion models struggle with a dilemma: inaccurate localization of concept-related representations causes unintended semantic interference, while incomplete removal of underlying concept knowledge allows adversarial recovery. There is a need for both precise and persistent concept erasure.
AI.method: PEAK trains a k-Sparse Autoencoder (kSAE) on internal activations of the diffusion denoising network to decompose dense representations into interpretable sparse features. It contrasts sparse activations from target vs. non-target prompts to identify target-specific features using both activation strength and frequency, then performs feature-guided parameter optimization that suppresses target-related activations while preserving non-target ones.
AI.result: On the I2P benchmark, PEAK reduces NudeNet detections from 582 to 6, lowers average attack success rate (ASR) from 96.52% to 5.63%, and preserves general generation quality on MS-COCO with near-zero KID.
AI.conclusion: PEAK achieves effective and robust concept erasure by embedding erasure directly into diffusion parameters, eliminating the need for inference-time intervention and providing persistence against adversarial attacks while maintaining generation quality.

title: Putting Registers to Work: Task Registers for Token Pruning in Vision Transformers
summary: Token-pruning policies are usually designed for a single recognition pipeline, but pretrained Vision Transformers are reused across tasks with different spatial demands. We ask which parts of a pruning policy transfer across image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection. For each pipeline, controlled probes freeze the no-pruning checkpoint and apply a series of parameter-free reduction criteria at one eligible layer at a time without retraining. The probes reveal three differences: segmentation and detection rank the criteria differently, classification is especially sensitive to attention-based pruning in the earliest layers, and the dense tasks prefer opposite recovery endpoints. These findings motivate Task-Adaptive Pruning (TAP). Existing register tokens serve as task-agnostic storage for feature artifacts. TAP instead introduces one task register per task and activates only the current one. Its evolving state ranks tokens, distributes an exact removal budget over depth, and sets the recovery scale for dense features. At a final keep rate of $ρ=0.5$, our jointly adapted model, TAP-J, reaches $47.0$ mIoU at $1.30\times$ encoder throughput on ADE20K and $53.7$ box AP at $1.32\times$ encoder throughput on COCO while remaining competitive on ImageNet-1K.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how token-pruning policies transfer across vision tasks (classification, segmentation, detection) and proposes Task-Adaptive Pruning (TAP), which introduces task-specific register tokens to adapt pruning decisions per task. TAP-J achieves strong efficiency gains on dense tasks (47.0 mIoU at 1.30x throughput on ADE20K, 53.7 box AP at 1.32x on COCO) while remaining competitive on ImageNet-1K at 50% keep rate.
AI.motivation: Token-pruning policies are typically designed for a single recognition pipeline, but pretrained Vision Transformers are reused across diverse tasks with different spatial demands (classification, segmentation, detection). It is unclear which parts of a pruning policy transfer across these tasks, motivating the need for task-adaptive pruning strategies.
AI.method: The authors use controlled probes that freeze the no-pruning checkpoint and apply parameter-free reduction criteria at one eligible layer at a time without retraining. These probes reveal task-specific differences in pruning behavior. Based on these findings, they propose TAP which introduces one task register per task (activated only for the current task) whose evolving state ranks tokens, distributes an exact removal budget over depth, and sets the recovery scale for dense features.
AI.result: At a keep rate of ρ=0.5, TAP-J achieves 47.0 mIoU at 1.30x encoder throughput on ADE20K, 53.7 box AP at 1.32x encoder throughput on COCO, while remaining competitive on ImageNet-1K classification.
AI.conclusion: Token-pruning policies do not transfer uniformly across vision tasks—dense tasks (segmentation, detection) require different pruning criteria, sensitivity patterns, and recovery endpoints than classification. Task-adaptive pruning with dedicated task registers enables effective, efficient inference across all three tasks from a single pretrained backbone.

title: HNDiff: Haze-Noise Diffusion for Image Dehazing
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project Page: https://jin-ting-he.github.io/HNDiff
summary: Existing diffusion-based methods have recently made significant progress in image dehazing. However, they typically neglect the physics of haze formation and reconstruct clean images from pure Gaussian noise, thereby limiting their restoration potential. To address this issue, we propose Haze-Noise Diffusion (HNDiff), a novel diffusion framework that embeds the atmospheric scattering model as an inductive bias. By grounding diffusion in physical principles, HNDiff ensures that the restoration aligns more closely with underlying mechanisms of haze formation. In its forward process, we introduce joint haze-noise diffusion with a haze-aware noise scheduler, which progressively adds both haze and noise to an image. Essentially, the scheduler adapts noise levels according to haze density, meaning that regions with heavier haze receive stronger noise injection to encourage content generation, while clearer regions receive lighter noise to better preserve details, which directly links the forward degradation process with the physics of haze. In the reverse process, we then derive a physically consistent dehazing-denoising process that simultaneously removes haze and noise to restore a clean image in a manner aligned with the forward degradation process. To further enhance practicality, we propose Latent HNDiff, which compiles clean latent priors that can be seamlessly integrated into existing dehazing networks to boost performance. Extensive experiments show that our work significantly improves leading dehazing backbones and achieves state-of-the-art results on benchmark datasets. The project page is available at https://jin-ting-he.github.io/HNDiff .

AI.tldr: HNDiff is a diffusion-based image dehazing framework that embeds the atmospheric scattering model as an inductive bias, using a haze-aware noise scheduler for joint haze-noise diffusion and a physically consistent reverse process, plus a Latent HNDiff variant that boosts existing dehazing networks.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based dehazing methods neglect the physics of haze formation and reconstruct clean images from pure Gaussian noise, limiting their restoration potential.
AI.method: HNDiff embeds the atmospheric scattering model as an inductive bias. Forward process: joint haze-noise diffusion with a haze-aware noise scheduler that adapts noise injection levels according to haze density (heavier haze gets more noise, clearer regions get less). Reverse process: a physically consistent dehazing-denoising process that removes haze and noise together. Also proposes Latent HNDiff, which compiles clean latent priors that can be integrated into existing dehazing networks.
AI.result: HNDiff significantly improves leading dehazing backbones and achieves state-of-the-art results on benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: Grounding diffusion in physical principles of haze formation improves dehazing performance and can boost existing networks via latent priors.

title: Watching Synthetic Videos: Aligning Cross-modal Representations with Visual Synthesis for Zero-shot Video Captioning
summary: Text-only training is a popular paradigm in zero-shot video captioning, where the video distribution is not available to the model during training, leading to a cross-modal gap between the training (text-only) and the inference (video-only). Previous works attempt to bridge the gap through simple linear transformations. However, the inherent gap between text and video makes cross-modal representation space alignment insufficient, resulting in inaccurate sentences. To address this issue, we propose a novel zero-shot video captioning framework (WSV) consisting of two training stages, which first generates corresponding synthetic video latent representations via a pretrained text-to-video generation model. To strengthen the fidelity of the latent representations, we propose a polisher capable of bridging the gap between real and synthetic video distributions. Subsequently, we design a prompter that conditions GPT-2 on the polished latent representations to generate the captions in the second training stage. During inference, an input video is encoded by a pretrained 3D Causal VAE and then fed directly into the prompter, which in turn guides GPT-2 to produce the final caption. Experimental results conducted on MSVD, MSR-VTT, and VATEX datasets demonstrate that our proposed method achieves scores of 52 and 95.7 on the B@4 and CIDEr metrics, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes WSV, a two-stage zero-shot video captioning framework that bridges the text-video gap by first generating synthetic video latents using a text-to-video model with a polisher to improve fidelity, then training a prompter to condition GPT-2 on these latents for caption generation. It achieves strong results on MSVD, MSR-VTT, and VATEX.
AI.motivation: Text-only training in zero-shot video captioning suffers from a cross-modal gap between training (text) and inference (video) data. Previous linear transformation approaches are insufficient for aligning text and video representation spaces, leading to inaccurate captions.
AI.method: The framework (WSV) consists of two training stages: (1) generating synthetic video latent representations via a pretrained text-to-video generation model, enhanced by a polisher that bridges real and synthetic video distribution gaps; (2) training a prompter that conditions GPT-2 on the polished latent representations to generate captions. At inference, input video is encoded by a 3D Causal VAE and fed directly into the prompter to guide GPT-2 caption generation.
AI.result: Experiments on MSVD, MSR-VTT, and VATEX datasets show the method achieves scores of 52 (B@4) and 95.7 (CIDEr).
AI.conclusion: The proposed two-stage framework effectively addresses the cross-modal gap in zero-shot video captioning by generating and polishing synthetic video latents, enabling improved caption quality compared to simple linear transformation approaches.

title: R4DSG: Relative 4D Scene Graph Memory for Object-Centric Question Answering in Long Egocentric Video
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, ACM Multimedia 2026, egocentric video; 3D scene graph; temporal memory; graph retrieval; object-state reasoning; multimodal question answering
summary: Long-horizon egocentric video is a rich substrate for wearable AI assistants, but object-centric questions such as where an item was moved, when it last changed state, or why it was relocated remain difficult because caption- and transcript-based memories rarely preserve persistent object identity or structured spatial change. Existing long-video QA methods mainly emphasize temporal grounding and clip retrieval, while prior 3D scene-graph methods typically assume stronger geometry than free-motion wearable RGB video provides, including point clouds, RGB-D input, posed views, sparse reconstruction, or reconstructed scenes. R4DSG introduces a relative 4D scene graph memory for long egocentric video. Instead of storing raw graph sequences, R4DSG converts video into compact queryable memory entries indexed by time, place, persistent objects, anchor-relative change, and local interaction context. The main idea is to separate stable anchors from dynamic objects, maintain persistent object identity across frames, and represent object state through anchor-relative transitions rather than a globally aligned world model. Built on recent RGB-only advances in promptable video segmentation, temporal propagation, and relative 3D lifting, the method produces a retrieval-ready memory directly usable for long-horizon question answering. Evaluation on a 255-question object-related subset from EgoLifeQA shows, under question-only retrieval, a 6.7-point overall gain over EgoRAG-Text and a 12.5-point gain on when questions, which highlights the value of temporally organized object memory. These results position relative 4D scene graphs as a practical memory substrate for wearable assistants, AR systems, and embodied multimedia agents. GitHub Page: https://dualtransparency.github.io/R4DSG/.

AI.tldr: R4DSG introduces a relative 4D scene graph memory for long egocentric video, converting video into compact queryable memory entries indexed by time, place, persistent objects, anchor-relative change, and local interaction context. It separates stable anchors from dynamic objects, maintains persistent object identity, and represents state changes via anchor-relative transitions rather than global world models. Built on RGB-only advances (promptable video segmentation, temporal propagation, relative 3D lifting), it achieves a 6.7-point gain over EgoRAG-Text on object-related questions and a 12.5-point gain on "when" questions in EgoLifeQA.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon egocentric video question answering is difficult because existing caption- and transcript-based memories don't preserve persistent object identity or structured spatial change. Prior long-video QA focuses on temporal grounding/clip retrieval, while 3D scene-graph methods assume stronger geometry (point clouds, RGB-D, posed views) than free-motion wearable RGB video provides. There is a need for a memory representation that handles object-centric queries in unconstrained egocentric video.
AI.method: R4DSG builds a relative 4D scene graph memory by (1) separating stable anchors from dynamic objects, (2) maintaining persistent object identity across frames, and (3) representing object state through anchor-relative transitions instead of a globally aligned world model. It converts video into queryable memory entries indexed by time, place, persistent objects, anchor-relative change, and local interaction context, using RGB-only techniques including promptable video segmentation, temporal propagation, and relative 3D lifting.
AI.result: On a 255-question object-related subset from EgoLifeQA, R4DSG achieves a 6.7-point overall gain over EgoRAG-Text under question-only retrieval, and a 12.5-point gain specifically on "when" questions.
AI.conclusion: Relative 4D scene graphs serve as a practical and effective memory substrate for wearable assistants, AR systems, and embodied multimedia agents, enabling object-centric long-horizon question answering from free-motion egocentric RGB video.

title: When Visual Signals Mislead: A Mechanistic Study of Attribute Hallucination in Vision-Language Models
summary: Attribute hallucination---where vision-language models (VLMs) correctly identify an object but mischaracterize its properties---is prevalent yet mechanistically poorly understood. The dominant explanation, language-prior dominance, has motivated prior-suppression methods, but this explanation has not been directly tested at the attribute level. We present VISOR (Visual-Operational Remediation), a unified framework that couples null-image-based diagnosis with routed remediation. Its VSNR diagnostic decomposes each prediction into a visual logit signal and a language-prior signal. Across 10,791 negative-ground-truth samples from three VLM families and three attribute types, the visual signal strongly predicts false positives, whereas the language-prior signal is near chance. VISOR uses this diagnosis to separate two failure modes: low-margin but directionally correct visual signals in color/state attributes, and low-SNR or misaligned visual signals in material attributes. The same diagnosis routes each query to the appropriate operator: calibration for threshold-placement errors, abstention for training-free low-SNR handling, or targeted visual adaptation for material failures that prior suppression cannot correct. Across Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA, VISOR reduces attribute false positives without relying on the prior-dominance assumption.

AI.tldr: VISOR is a unified framework combining null-image-based diagnosis (VSNR) with routed remediation to address attribute hallucination in VLMs, showing that visual signal failures—not language-prior dominance—are the primary cause, and applying targeted fixes (calibration, abstention, or visual adaptation) reduces false positives across Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA.
AI.motivation: Attribute hallucination in VLMs is prevalent but poorly understood; the dominant language-prior dominance explanation has never been directly tested at the attribute level, motivating a rigorous diagnostic approach.
AI.method: VISOR introduces VSNR (Visual-Operational Remediation with Signal-to-Noise Ratio) diagnosis that decomposes each prediction into visual logit and language-prior signals using null images, then routes each failure mode to appropriate operators: calibration, abstention, or visual adaptation.
AI.result: Across 10,791 negative-ground-truth samples from three VLM families and three attribute types, the visual signal strongly predicts false positives while language-prior signal is near chance; VISOR reduces attribute false positives across Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA.
AI.conclusion: The language-prior dominance assumption is incorrect for attribute hallucination; failures stem from low-margin, low-SNR, or misaligned visual signals, and targeted remediation based on diagnosis is more effective than prior suppression.

title: Multi-Level Evidence Aggregation for Robust Facial Phenotype Retrieval in Rare Genetic Disorder Prioritization
comment: including supplementary notes: 32 pages, 16 figures. Preprint submitted to journal for peer-review
summary:
AI-assisted facial phenotyping supports rare genetic disorder prioritization by retrieving visually similar diagnosed cases from facial image reference databases such as the GestaltMatcher Database (GMDB). Existing GestaltMatcher-based retrieval frameworks compare each test image with individual gallery images in a facial phenotype embedding space. However, this pointwise formulation does not fully exploit available evidence, because patients may have multiple images and disorders may be represented by multiple diagnosed gallery patients.
  We propose an inference-time multi-level evidence aggregation framework that improves facial phenotype retrieval without modifying the underlying GestaltMatcher-Arc encoder. The framework combines embedding-level patient aggregation of multiple images from the same individual, patient-weighted disorder centroids, and hybrid individual-centroid scoring to integrate test-patient observations, disorder-level gallery evidence, and local nearest-neighbor evidence.
  We evaluated the approach on GMDB v1.1.4 across disorders represented during training (GMDB-Freq), unseen disorders (GMDB-Rare), and multi-image patient subsets, using a unified gallery containing both GMDB-Freq and GMDB-Rare disorders. Multi-level evidence aggregation improved mean per-disorder top-$N$ retrieval accuracy across all evaluation subsets. Top-1 accuracy increased from 38.52% to 48.82% on GMDB-Freq and from 19.38% to 23.79% on GMDB-Rare. On multi-image subsets, top-1 accuracy increased from 46.12% to 60.94% on GMDB-Multi-Freq and from 18.54% to 26.71% on GMDB-Multi-Rare.
  These findings show that inference-time aggregation can improve next-generation facial phenotype retrieval without retraining the encoder, supporting a shift from isolated single-image matching toward multi-level aggregation of patient and disorder evidence for rare-disorder prioritization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an inference-time multi-level evidence aggregation framework that improves facial phenotype retrieval for rare genetic disorder prioritization by combining embedding-level patient aggregation, patient-weighted disorder centroids, and hybrid individual-centroid scoring—without retraining the underlying GestaltMatcher-Arc encoder. The method achieves significant top-1 accuracy improvements across both frequently-seen and rare disorder subsets in GMDB.
AI.motivation: Existing GestaltMatcher-based retrieval compares each test image with individual gallery images in a pointwise manner, which fails to fully exploit available evidence—patients may have multiple images and disorders may be represented by multiple diagnosed gallery patients. This underutilization of evidence limits retrieval performance.
AI.method: The framework operates at inference time without modifying the GestaltMatcher-Arc encoder. It combines: (1) embedding-level patient aggregation of multiple images from the same individual, (2) patient-weighted disorder centroids, and (3) hybrid individual-centroid scoring that integrates test-patient observations, disorder-level gallery evidence, and local nearest-neighbor evidence.
AI.result: On GMDB v1.1.4, the method improved mean per-disorder top-N retrieval accuracy across all evaluation subsets. Top-1 accuracy increased from 38.52% to 48.82% on GMDB-Freq, from 19.38% to 23.79% on GMDB-Rare, from 46.12% to 60.94% on GMDB-Multi-Freq, and from 18.54% to 26.71% on GMDB-Multi-Rare.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time aggregation can substantially improve facial phenotype retrieval without retraining the encoder, supporting a paradigm shift from isolated single-image matching toward multi-level aggregation of patient and disorder evidence for rare-disorder prioritization.

title: 3D Weighted Geometric Graph Neural Networks for Sheep Facial Pain Assessment
summary: Deep learning systems perform mainly within the 2D for a single image domain and take the face as a single-dimension representation, losing sight of the 3D anatomy of sheep and cross-landmark spatial relationships that are intrinsic to the clinically proven Sheep Pain Facial Expression Scale (SPFES). This paper presents the \textbf{3D Sheep Pain Facial Expression System (3D-SPFES)}, a novel, monocular depth-aware geometric graph neural network system that integrates each SPFES facial landmark, such as the ears, eyes, and nose, into 3D Euclidean space estimated from a single RGB camera by using VideoDepthAnything, thus preventing the need for specialized depth hardware. Each landmark node includes a feature vector containing its 3D spatial coordinates, estimated surface normal, and facial attribute class embedding. Edges linked to nodes are assigned weights based on an aggregate metric that combines both Euclidean distance and surface co-planarity in a 3D space.
