A Weighted Geometric Graph Neural Network (WG-GNN) studies this graph using $\mathcal{K} = 3$ geometry-aware message-passing layers enhanced by a scaled dot-product attention method that selectively enhances anatomically relevant inter-landmark messages. The resultant node embeddings are combined into $\mathcal{O} = 3$ pain-level clusters and integrated into a Normalized Pain Score (NPS) within the range of $[0, 100%]$ a confidence-weighted, SPFES-derived scoring method.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces 3D-SPFES, a monocular depth-aware geometric graph neural network that estimates 3D facial landmarks of sheep from a single RGB camera to assess pain levels based on the Sheep Pain Facial Expression Scale (SPFES). It builds a 3D geometric graph using depth estimation (VideoDepthAnything), applies a weighted geometric GNN with attention-based message passing, and outputs pain-level clusters converted into a normalized pain score.
AI.motivation: Traditional deep learning systems analyze sheep pain using 2D single-image face representations, overlooking the 3D anatomy and cross-landmark spatial relationships that are fundamental to the clinically validated Sheep Pain Facial Expression Scale (SPFES). This paper aims to bridge that gap by incorporating 3D geometric information without requiring specialized depth hardware.
AI.method: The system (3D-SPFES) estimates 3D coordinates of SPFES facial landmarks (ears, eyes, nose) from a single RGB camera using VideoDepthAnything. Each landmark node contains a feature vector of 3D spatial coordinates, estimated surface normal, and facial attribute class embedding. Graph edges are weighted by an aggregate metric combining Euclidean distance and surface co-planarity in 3D space. A Weighted Geometric Graph Neural Network (WG-GNN) processes the graph using K=3 geometry-aware message-passing layers with scaled dot-product attention. Node embeddings are clustered into O=3 pain levels and integrated into a Normalized Pain Score (NPS) in [0,100%].
AI.result: The paper proposes a confidence-weighted, SPFES-derived scoring method that produces a Normalized Pain Score (NPS) ranging from 0 to 100%, derived from three pain-level clusters built from the learned node embeddings.
AI.conclusion: The 3D-SPFES provides a novel approach to sheep pain assessment that respects the 3D anatomical structure and cross-landmark spatial relationships intrinsic to the SPFES, while remaining practical by requiring only a single RGB camera instead of specialized depth sensors.

title: HUI360: A 360° Egocentric Dataset and Baselines for Human-Robot Interaction Anticipation
summary: As robots increasingly operate in human-populated environments, anticipating human intentions is essential for enabling proactive and socially aware behavior. Automatic anticipation of human-robot interactions is thus emerging as a crucial perception challenge for embodied agents. To this end, we introduce HUI360, the largest dataset for human-robot interaction anticipation in the wild and its set of baselines. The dataset was collected from a mobile robot, in the wild, over multiple days within a 3-month period, and in several environments, capturing natural, spontaneous behaviors from both passersby and users, and encompassing a diverse range of individuals. This variety enables evaluating and improving the generalization capabilities of interaction anticipation models. We designed a pipeline and share code for automatic interaction annotation in arbitrary 360-degree equirectangular videos, along with interfaces for manual refinement. Using this pipeline, we release the HUI360 open set of 1M pre-processed annotations, including detailed 2D poses, facial keypoints, and segmentation masks, obtained using state-of-the-art computer vision methods and manually curated to ensure high-quality tracking and interaction annotation. Additionally, we release the raw panoptic 360-degree images captured from the robot's egocentric viewpoint (on demand, for research purpose only in compliance with GDPR). Finally, we establish benchmark baselines for interaction anticipation, including the first cross-dataset evaluations for this task: to this end, we also release 6M annotations for another existing in-the-wild outdoor dataset collected from a mobile robot (SSUP-HRI). Dataset and code can be found at https://hucebot.github.io/hui360.

AI.tldr: HUI360 is the largest in-the-wild human-robot interaction (HRI) anticipation dataset, collected from a mobile robot over 3 months across multiple environments. It includes 1M curated annotations (2D poses, facial keypoints, segmentation masks) with a full annotation pipeline, plus 6M additional annotations from the SSUP-HRI dataset. Baseline benchmarks include the first cross-dataset evaluations for interaction anticipation.
AI.motivation: As robots operate in human-populated environments, anticipating human intentions is critical for proactive and socially aware behavior. However, existing datasets lack scale, diversity, and in-the-wild natural behaviors needed to train and evaluate interaction anticipation models effectively.
AI.method: The authors collected a large in-the-wild dataset from a mobile robot over several days across multiple environments within a 3-month period. They designed an automatic annotation pipeline for 360-degree equirectangular videos (with manual refinement interfaces), used state-of-the-art computer vision methods to generate 2D poses, facial keypoints, and segmentation masks, and manually curated the annotations. They also annotated 6M additional frames from an existing outdoor dataset (SSUP-HRI) and established benchmark baselines including cross-dataset evaluations.
AI.result: The dataset contains 1M pre-processed annotations with 2D poses, facial keypoints, and segmentation masks, plus 6M annotations from the SSUP-HRI dataset. The authors provide the first cross-dataset evaluation baselines for interaction anticipation, along with the largest HRI anticipation dataset collected in natural, unscripted settings.
AI.conclusion: HUI360 provides a comprehensive, large-scale resource for human-robot interaction anticipation research, enabling evaluation of model generalization across diverse real-world environments and facilitating future progress in proactive social robot behavior.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of Deep Learning Object Detection Models on a Real-World Multi-Plant Dataset from Africa
summary: The application of computer vision in agriculture has shown significant potential for improving crop monitoring and precision farming. However, many existing approaches rely on controlled datasets that do not adequately represent realworld farming conditions, particularly in underrepresented regions such as Africa. This study presents a comparative evaluation of six object detection models YOLOv5, YOLOv8, YOLO11, YOLO26, Faster R-CNN, and RT-DETR using a real-world dataset, AgriAISeg 1 , collected manually from Nigerian farms. AgriAISeg comprises 3,382 images of sesame, cabbage, and tomato crops captured under varying environmental conditions, including changes in illumination, occlusion, and viewing perspectives. Models were trained, and performance was assessed using precision, recall, mAP@0.5, and mAP@0.5:0.95. The results show that RT-DETR achieved the highest overall performance with a precision of 0.768 and mAP@0.5:0.95 of 0.624, while YOLOv8 and YOLO11 also demonstrated strong and consistent performance. In contrast, Faster R-CNN recorded significantly lower accuracy, with an overall mAP@0.5 of 0.466, indicating reduced effectiveness under complex field conditions. In addition, YOLO-based models exhibited superior training efficiency compared to Faster R-CNN.These findings demonstrate that modern one-stage and transformer-based detectors provide more reliable and efficient solutions for plant detection in realworld agricultural environments.

AI.tldr: This paper compares six object detection models (YOLOv5, YOLOv8, YOLO11, YOLO26, Faster R-CNN, RT-DETR) on a real-world agricultural dataset (AgriAISeg) collected from Nigerian farms, finding RT-DETR achieves the best performance while YOLO variants offer superior training efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing computer vision approaches for agriculture rely on controlled datasets that fail to represent real-world farming conditions, particularly in underrepresented regions like Africa. There is a need to evaluate detection models on realistic, challenging field data.
AI.method: Six object detection models were trained and evaluated on AgriAISeg, a manually collected real-world dataset of 3,382 images of sesame, cabbage, and tomato crops with varying illumination, occlusion, and viewing perspectives. Performance was measured using precision, recall, mAP@0.5, and mAP@0.5:0.95, along with training efficiency comparisons.
AI.result: RT-DETR achieved the highest overall performance (precision 0.768, mAP@0.5:0.95 of 0.624). YOLOv8 and YOLO11 showed strong, consistent performance. Faster R-CNN performed significantly worse (mAP@0.5 of 0.466). YOLO-based models demonstrated superior training efficiency compared to Faster R-CNN.
AI.conclusion: Modern one-stage and transformer-based detectors provide more reliable and efficient solutions for plant detection in real-world agricultural environments compared to traditional two-stage detectors like Faster R-CNN.

title: Entropy-Centric Explainable AI for Remote Sensing Image Segmentation
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a powerful approach to solving complex problems in critical domains. Many concerns arise regarding the decision-making process of its models, mainly due to deep neural networks outperforming their peers at the cost of ambiguity in feature extraction and prediction. Consequently, in critical domains such as remote sensing, where high-resolution imagery must be analyzed using black-box models, the lack of transparency limits trust in these models and, thus, their adoption. In light of this reality, explaining and understanding the complex decision-making process of AI models has become essential. Explainable AI (XAI) aims to bridge this gap by providing insights into how and why certain decisions are made. While significant progress has been achieved in explaining image classification tasks, image segmentation still offers considerable room for improvement. In this context, this paper proposes an entropy-centric XAI method for semantic segmentation. Moreover, a new XAI evaluation methodology is proposed to efficiently measure the relevance of the regions highlighted by the proposed XAI method. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed XAI method compared with recently adapted XAI methods for semantic segmentation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an entropy-centric Explainable AI (XAI) method for semantic segmentation in remote sensing, along with a new evaluation methodology to measure the relevance of highlighted regions. The method demonstrates superiority over recently adapted XAI approaches for semantic segmentation.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks used in critical domains like remote sensing suffer from opacity in their decision-making processes, limiting trust and adoption. While XAI has made progress for image classification, semantic segmentation still lacks effective explanation methods, motivating the need for improved XAI approaches and evaluation metrics in this area.
AI.method: The paper proposes an entropy-centric XAI method specifically designed for semantic segmentation tasks, and introduces a novel XAI evaluation methodology to efficiently assess the relevance of the regions highlighted by the proposed explanation method.
AI.result: Experimental results show that the proposed entropy-centric XAI method outperforms recently adapted XAI methods for semantic segmentation, as validated through the newly proposed evaluation methodology.
AI.conclusion: The entropy-centric XAI method provides a more effective approach for explaining semantic segmentation models in critical domains such as remote sensing, with the proposed evaluation methodology enabling more reliable assessment of explanation quality. This contributes to improving transparency and trust in AI-based decision-making.

title: CapProbe: Evaluating Detailed Image Captions via Full-Scene Dense Question Answering
summary: Evaluating detailed image captions from Vision-Language Models (VLMs) requires going beyond surface-level semantic similarity. Reference-based metrics (e.g., CIDEr and SPICE) and LLM-as-scorer protocols struggle to verify dense factual claims, while existing QA-based alternatives generally offer lower probe density, narrower domain coverage, or no explicit alignment between individual questions and segmented image regions. We introduce CapProbe, a full-scene dense QA benchmark that turns detailed caption evaluation into region-aligned factual checking. Each image is decomposed into coarse semantic regions covering both foreground and background elements; for every retained region, we generate multiple-choice questions spanning 10 semantic categories, forming a dense checklist of probed visual facts. Guided by a two-tier taxonomy of 37 L1 domains and 219 L2 sub-domains, CapProbe comprises 346 images, 1,868 regions, and 25,650 questions, averaging 74 QA pairs per image. A language judge answers from the caption alone; an Uncertain option and Effective Accuracy provide a judge-dependent proxy for distinguishing unanswered probes from incorrectly resolved ones, while density-based metrics penalize verbose yet uninformative captions. The protocol is cost-effective: by converting unconstrained scalar scoring into structured MCQ reading, it reduces open-ended scoring bias while remaining judge-conditioned and yields relatively stable model rankings under a fixed reader. Experiments on 13 VLMs show large Coverage gaps across models, a clear competency-efficiency trade-off, and failure modes that sparse or overlap-based evaluation often misses. The benchmark data, annotations, and evaluation code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: CapProbe is a full-scene dense QA benchmark that evaluates VLM image captioning by decomposing each image into semantic regions and generating a dense checklist of multiple-choice questions (10 semantic categories, 37 L1/219 L2 taxonomy domains) — 346 images, 1,868 regions, 25,650 questions. A language judge answers from the caption alone, with an Uncertain option and Effective Accuracy metric to distinguish unanswered vs. incorrectly resolved probes, plus density-based metrics to penalize verbose uninformative captions.
AI.motivation: Existing metrics (CIDEr, SPICE, LLM-as-scorer) and QA-based alternatives struggle to verify dense factual claims in detailed image captions due to low probe density, narrow domain coverage, or lack of alignment between questions and image regions.
AI.method: Images are decomposed into coarse semantic regions (foreground and background). For each region, multiple-choice questions are generated across 10 semantic categories, guided by a two-tier taxonomy (37 L1 domains, 219 L2 sub-domains). A language judge reads the caption and answers questions, with an Uncertain option provided. Effective Accuracy distinguishes unanswered from incorrectly resolved probes, and density-based metrics penalize verbose uninformative captions.
AI.result: Experiments on 13 VLMs reveal large Coverage gaps across models, a clear competency-efficiency trade-off, and failure modes that sparse or overlap-based evaluation misses.
AI.conclusion: CapProbe provides a cost-effective, judge-conditioned protocol that reduces open-ended scoring bias, yields stable model rankings under a fixed reader, and complements existing evaluation approaches by capturing dense factual coverage that other metrics miss.

title: Static in Frames, Dynamic in Events: Rethinking Features in Event Cameras as Motion Cues
summary: Event cameras capture intensity changes asynchronously with high temporal resolution, requiring novel preprocessing methods for downstream tasks. Unlike static intensity snapshots, event data inherently encode information about scene dynamics and object motion, meaning that features derived from events can exhibit behaviors with no direct analogue in frame-based vision. In this paper, we analyze two features used in event-based corner detection---the eigenvalues of the structure tensor and the spatiotemporal density values---and show that they are \emph{motion cues}. We hypothesize that these features, combined with local geometric information, can enhance motion estimation tasks. To validate this, we first theoretically analyze how the eigenvalues of the structure tensor at moving corner points relate to the direction of motion. We then design controlled experiments on a synthetic dataset, confirming that extending local geometric features with eigenvalues and density values provides complementary motion information and is robust to texture and shot noise. Finally, we integrate the proposed features into a state-of-the-art event-based optical flow network and evaluate on the real-world DSEC benchmark, where the added features consistently improve accuracy, with the largest gains in data-scarce scenarios and for lower-capacity models. The code for this paper can be found at: \href{https://github.com/hesamaraghi/static-in-frames-dynamic-in-events}{https://github.com/hesamaraghi/static-in-frames-dynamic-in-events}.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes two features used in event-based corner detection—eigenvalues of the structure tensor and spatiotemporal density values—and shows they are motion cues. The authors theoretically analyze how these features relate to motion direction at moving corner points, validate their hypothesis with controlled synthetic experiments, and integrate the features into a state-of-the-art event-based optical flow network, demonstrating consistent accuracy improvements on the DSEC benchmark, especially in data-scarce scenarios and for lower-capacity models.
AI.motivation: Event cameras capture intensity changes asynchronously and inherently encode scene dynamics and object motion, unlike static frame-based vision. Features derived from events may exhibit behaviors with no direct analogue in frame-based vision, yet this motion-related nature of event-based features has not been systematically analyzed or exploited for downstream tasks like motion estimation.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze how the eigenvalues of the structure tensor at moving corner points relate to motion direction. They then design controlled experiments on a synthetic dataset to confirm that extending local geometric features with eigenvalue and density features provides complementary motion information robust to texture and shot noise. Finally, they integrate these features into a state-of-the-art event-based optical flow network and evaluate on the real-world DSEC benchmark.
AI.result: The added features consistently improve optical flow accuracy on the DSEC benchmark, with the largest gains observed in data-scarce scenarios and for lower-capacity models. Synthetic experiments confirm the features provide complementary motion information and are robust to texture and shot noise.
AI.conclusion: Features traditionally used for event-based corner detection (structure tensor eigenvalues and spatiotemporal density) are motion cues that, when combined with local geometric information, can enhance event-based motion estimation tasks.

title: Foundation Model-Enabled Efficient Data Sampling (FEEDS): A label-efficient training strategy for pan-cancer, multi-tracer PET/CT datasets
summary: Automated lesion segmentation in whole-body PET/CT imaging can assist clinicians with cancer detection, staging, and treatment planning across radiotracers and cancer types. However, training lesion segmentation models that capture variations in lesion size, distribution, and appearance requires large annotated datasets, whose creation is both time- and expertise-intensive. As a result, models trained on limited labeled PET/CT data often lack the accuracy and generalizability needed for clinical use. We present FEEDS (Foundation model-Enabled Efficient Data Sampling), a label- and compute-efficient learning strategy that uses vision foundation model embeddings to select the most informative and diverse unlabeled cases for expert annotation. Unlike unsupervised, semi-supervised, and active learning approaches, FEEDS is a one-step training paradigm requiring only a limited, representative training set, making it label- and compute-efficient. We train and validate FEEDS using the AutoPET-III dataset. We test its accuracy and generalizability on three held-out sets: AutoPET-III, DeepPSMA, and an internal Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center dataset. We evaluate clinical utility at the voxel, lesion, and anatomic region level to assess performance in high-risk areas and treatment planning utility. FEEDS outperforms random-sampling-based labeling, pseudolabel-based semi-supervised learning, and training with limited labeled data alone. It generalizes across all three test sets, FDG and PSMA tracers, and multiple diseases, matching fully-labeled (100\%) training performance with 70\% less annotation burden. FEEDS addresses the challenge of label scarcity in an automatic lesion segmentation framework by providing a practical approach for constructing representative and diverse annotation queues from large, unannotated clinical repositories.

AI.tldr: FEEDS is a label- and compute-efficient learning strategy for automated lesion segmentation in whole-body PET/CT imaging that uses vision foundation model embeddings to select the most informative and diverse unlabeled cases for expert annotation. It matches fully-labeled training performance with 70% less annotation burden and generalizes across multiple datasets, tracers, and diseases.
AI.motivation: Training lesion segmentation models for whole-body PET/CT imaging requires large annotated datasets, which are time- and expertise-intensive to create. Models trained on limited labeled data often lack the accuracy and generalizability needed for clinical use, creating a need for a more efficient labeling strategy.
AI.method: FEEDS uses vision foundation model embeddings to select the most informative and diverse unlabeled cases for expert annotation in a one-step training paradigm. Unlike unsupervised, semi-supervised, or active learning approaches, it requires only a limited, representative training set. The method was trained and validated using the AutoPET-III dataset.
AI.result: FEEDS outperforms random-sampling-based labeling, pseudolabel-based semi-supervised learning, and training with limited labeled data alone. It generalizes across three held-out test sets (AutoPET-III, DeepPSMA, and Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center), FDG and PSMA tracers, and multiple diseases, matching fully-labeled training performance with 70% less annotation burden.
AI.conclusion: FEEDS addresses the challenge of label scarcity in automatic lesion segmentation frameworks by providing a practical approach for constructing representative and diverse annotation queues from large, unannotated clinical repositories.

title: Learning Gaussian Structure: Intervention-Guided Density Control for Feed-Forward Driving Reconstruction
summary: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction has recently emerged as an efficient approach for driving scene reconstruction. However, prevailing LiDAR-based methods preserve the initial correspondence between observed points and Gaussian primitives, treating the initialized primitive set as the final representation. Unlike optimization-based 3DGS, these methods cannot accumulate gradients during training to determine how the scenes representation should be densified. Meanwhile, the shared sparse backbone only fuses observations from different timestamps implicitly, without explicitly aggregating cross-time evidence for individual primitives. In this paper, we present Learning Gaussian Structure (LGS), a framework that enhances both Gaussian structure and primitive attributes. Our key observation is that changes in local gradient responses induced by a prune or add intervention reveal whether the corresponding structural adjustment benefits reconstruction. Based on this observation, our Gaussian Densify Policy learns a Densify Map comprising Prune and Addition Scores from controlled interventions, and directly adjusts the Gaussian structure during inference. We further develop a compact Cross-Time Point Query that explicitly retrieves and aggregates neighboring features from Gaussian primitives at other timestamps for reliable attribute prediction. Extensive experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset and PandaSet demonstrate that LGS consistently outperforms existing methods.

AI.tldr: LGS is a framework for feed-forward LiDAR-based Gaussian reconstruction that learns to densify/prune Gaussian primitives via a policy derived from controlled gradient interventions, and improves attribute prediction through explicit cross-time feature aggregation.
AI.motivation: Existing LiDAR-based feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction methods fix the initial point-to-primitive correspondence, preventing gradient-based densification that optimization-based 3DGS enjoys. Additionally, the shared sparse backbone only fuses multi-timestamp observations implicitly, lacking explicit cross-time evidence aggregation for individual primitives.
AI.method: LGS introduces (1) a Gaussian Densify Policy that learns a Densify Map (Prune and Addition Scores) from controlled prune/add interventions by observing local gradient responses, enabling direct structural adjustment during inference; and (2) a compact Cross-Time Point Query that explicitly retrieves and aggregates neighboring features from Gaussian primitives at other timestamps for better attribute prediction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Waymo Open Dataset and PandaSet show LGS consistently outperforms existing feed-forward LiDAR-based Gaussian reconstruction methods.
AI.conclusion: Learning both Gaussian structure (via densify policy) and primitive attributes (via cross-time query) yields superior reconstruction performance over current baselines, demonstrating the benefit of explicit structure adaptation and temporal feature aggregation.

title: Every Packet Counts: Dispersing Information for Loss-Resilient Learned Image Compression
comment: 16 pages, 12 figures, 8 tables. Joint first authors: Yuhang Wei and Chuqin Zhou. Corresponding author: Guo Lu. To appear in Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '26), November 10-14, 2026, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
summary: Learned image compression (LIC) has achieved impressive rate-distortion performance. However, existing methods remain highly vulnerable to packet loss, a common challenge in satellite and emergency communications. This vulnerability stems from non-uniform information distribution at the packetization stage and sequential decoding dependencies at the entropy coding stage. We propose an end-to-end loss-resilient image compression scheme that addresses both. Before packetization, we introduce an Inter-Channel Redistribution (ICR) mechanism to redistribute channel energy, preventing critical information concentrating in a small subset of channels. Then, an Interleaved Channel Grouping (ICG) strategy partitions latent channels in a strided manner to disperse information across packets, with each packet kept within constrained sizes. To limit cascading errors from lost packets, we adopt a two-layer dual-branch autoregressive structure to shorten the dependency chain. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing approaches in both reconstruction quality and stability. At 20% packet loss, it achieves an average PSNR gain of 1.84 dB over LossResilientLIC while reducing PSNR variance by an order of magnitude. Notably, trained under uniform random loss only, our model generalizes to bursty loss modeled by the Gilbert-Elliott channel, outperforming methods explicitly trained for such conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an end-to-end loss-resilient learned image compression scheme. It addresses packet loss vulnerability in LIC by introducing Inter-Channel Redistribution (ICR) to prevent critical information concentration, Interleaved Channel Grouping (ICG) to disperse information across packets, and a two-layer dual-branch autoregressive structure to shorten decoding dependency chains. The method achieves 1.84 dB PSNR gain at 20% packet loss over LossResilientLIC, reduces PSNR variance by an order of magnitude, and generalizes to bursty loss despite only being trained under uniform random loss.
AI.motivation: Existing learned image compression methods achieve excellent rate-distortion performance but remain highly vulnerable to packet loss, a common challenge in satellite and emergency communications. This vulnerability stems from two root causes: non-uniform information distribution during packetization and sequential decoding dependencies in entropy coding. Existing methods fail to address both issues simultaneously.
AI.method: The proposed loss-resilient scheme consists of three key components: (1) Inter-Channel Redistribution (ICR) redistributes channel energy before packetization to prevent critical information from concentrating in a small subset of channels; (2) Interleaved Channel Grouping (ICG) partitions latent channels in a strided manner to disperse information across packets, keeping each packet within constrained sizes; (3) a two-layer dual-branch autoregressive structure limits cascading errors from lost packets by shortening the dependency chain.
AI.result: At 20% packet loss, the method achieves an average PSNR gain of 1.84 dB over LossResilientLIC while reducing PSNR variance by an order of magnitude. Trained only under uniform random loss, the model generalizes to bursty loss modeled by the Gilbert-Elliott channel, outperforming methods explicitly trained for such conditions. The method consistently outperforms existing approaches in both reconstruction quality and stability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed end-to-end loss-resilient image compression scheme effectively addresses packet loss vulnerability in learned image compression by tackling both information concentration during packetization and sequential decoding dependencies. The approach demonstrates superior reconstruction quality and stability, with strong generalization to bursty channel conditions beyond its training distribution.

title: AlbumentationsX: One Augmentation Pipeline for Images and Related Annotations
summary:
Augmentation can corrupt a training example when an image and its annotations receive different random changes. A crop must use the same coordinates for the image, mask, boxes, keypoints, stereo views, video frames, or volume. Code paths that choose these values separately can silently misalign the data.
  AlbumentationsX keeps the transform list, probabilities, annotation settings, and random seed in one Compose object. Each call chooses random values once and applies them to every supported part of the training example. The library keeps each object's mask, box, and label together and lets projects add their own transforms. It can also save the pipeline definition, show what happened in one call, and run that call again.
  The examples place Compose after files have been decoded into arrays and before PyTorch groups examples into a batch. AlbumentationsX executes the declared transforms. Practitioners still decide whether a flip, crop, color change, or other operation preserves the correct label for their task.

AI.tldr: AlbumentationsX is a data augmentation library that prevents annotation-image misalignment by keeping all transforms, probabilities, and the random seed in a single Compose object, applying randomly chosen values consistently across all supported annotation types (masks, boxes, keypoints, etc.) within a training example.
AI.motivation: Data augmentation can corrupt training examples when images and their annotations (masks, boxes, keypoints, etc.) receive different random transformations, such as a crop applying different coordinates to the image versus its annotations, silently misaligning the data.
AI.method: AlbumentationsX centralizes the transform list, probabilities, annotation settings, and random seed into one Compose object. Each call selects random values once and applies them uniformly to every supported component of the training example. It keeps each object's mask, box, and label together, supports user-defined transforms, can save the pipeline definition, visualize what happened in a single call, and replay that call.
AI.result: The library addresses annotation misalignment by ensuring synchronized random transformations across all data components. It is designed to be placed after file decoding and before PyTorch batching, executing declared transforms while leaving task-specific label validity decisions to practitioners.
AI.conclusion: AlbumentationsX provides a unified augmentation pipeline that guarantees consistent transformation of images and all their annotations, though practitioners must still judge whether specific operations preserve label correctness for their particular task.

title: Is There Really a Camouflaged Object? Towards Realistic Camouflaged Object Detection
summary: Camouflaged object detection (COD) aims to segment objects that are visually concealed in their surroundings and has attracted increasing attention in recent years. However, most existing COD methods are developed under a closed-world assumption, where each input image is assumed to contain a camouflaged object. This assumption ignores realistic scenarios with pure backgrounds or non-camouflaged objects, causing existing models to produce severe false positives when deployed in open-world environments. To address this limitation, we propose OPC16K, a large-scale benchmark for realistic COD. OPC16K contains 16,245 images from 14 sources and is carefully organized into camouflaged-object images, pure background images, and non-camouflaged-object images, enabling comprehensive evaluation of both segmentation quality and negative-sample rejection. Based on this benchmark, we further propose OPCNet, a presence-aware camouflage network that reformulates COD from a pure segmentation task into a joint problem of object localization and camouflage existence reasoning. Specifically, OPCNet introduces hierarchical existence reasoning to distinguish CO, BG, and NOCOD scenarios, similarity-aware camouflage relation modeling to capture foreground-background camouflage cues, and existence-aware feature refinement to regulate segmentation features with existence predictions. Extensive experiments on OPC16K demonstrate that OPCNet achieves superior performance under the proposed realistic COD evaluation protocol, significantly reducing false positives on negative samples while maintaining accurate camouflaged-object segmentation. Code and dataset will be released at https://github.com/2231122/OPCOD.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OPC16K, a large-scale benchmark for realistic camouflaged object detection (COD) containing 16,245 images across camouflaged, pure background, and non-camouflaged categories, along with OPCNet, a presence-aware network that jointly handles object localization and camouflage existence reasoning, significantly reducing false positives in open-world scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing COD methods operate under a closed-world assumption where every input is assumed to contain a camouflaged object, which fails in realistic open-world scenarios involving pure backgrounds or non-camouflaged objects, leading to severe false positives.
AI.method: Proposes OPC16K benchmark with 16,245 images from 14 sources organized into camouflaged, pure background, and non-camouflaged categories. Introduces OPCNet with three key components: hierarchical existence reasoning to distinguish CO/BG/NOCOD scenarios, similarity-aware camouflage relation modeling to capture foreground-background camouflage cues, and existence-aware feature refinement to regulate segmentation features with existence predictions. The task is reformulated from pure segmentation into joint object localization and camouflage existence reasoning.
AI.result: OPCNet achieves superior performance on the OPC16K benchmark under the realistic COD evaluation protocol, significantly reducing false positives on negative samples while maintaining accurate camouflaged-object segmentation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed realistic COD evaluation protocol and OPCNet framework address the open-world limitation of existing COD methods, providing a more practical benchmark and solution for real-world camouflaged object detection applications.

title: SAR2Agri: Learning SAR Intensity Representations for Agricultural Monitoring
summary: Agricultural monitoring faces unique challenges, arising from the landscape's complex temporal, phenological, and climate dynamics, yet monitoring them is critical for ensuring food security. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites offer all-weather day-night imaging capability supporting key monitoring tasks including crop type mapping, yield prediction and phenological event detection. Existing multimodal remote sensing foundation models including TerraMind and CopernicusFM learn SAR representations by grounding them in optical imagery using joint encoding and contrastive learning techniques, while SAR-specific foundation models such as SAR-JEPA, SARMAE, and SAR-W-MixMAE primarily focus on target detection, flood mapping, and land cover classification applications. Recent work has introduced phenology inspired temporal pretext tasks with optical imagery which has shown strong performance on agricultural downstream tasks. In this work, we propose the first self-supervised learning pipeline focused on using only SAR intensity imagery for agricultural applications. We improve the temporal pretext tasks through masking and curriculum learning to enhance the pretraining pipeline's ability to capture phenological features from SAR. On the SICKLE benchmark, our final model achieves 84.9% IoU on crop type mapping, outperforming optical baselines (by 15.3 pt) and existing SAR baselines (by 2.2 pt), demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed pipeline for pretraining SAR intensity encoders for agricultural monitoring.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the first self-supervised learning pipeline using only SAR intensity imagery for agricultural applications. It improves temporal pretext tasks through masking and curriculum learning to capture phenological features, achieving 84.9% IoU on crop type mapping on the SICKLE benchmark, outperforming optical baselines by 15.3 points and SAR baselines by 2.2 points.
AI.motivation: Agricultural monitoring is critical for food security but faces challenges from complex temporal, phenological, and climate dynamics. While SAR satellites offer all-weather day-night imaging, existing multimodal and SAR-specific foundation models either rely on optical grounding or focus on non-agricultural tasks. There is a gap in SAR-only self-supervised learning methods tailored for agricultural applications that capture phenological features.
AI.method: The authors propose a self-supervised learning (SSL) pipeline that uses only SAR intensity imagery. They enhance temporal pretext tasks with masking and curriculum learning to better capture phenological features from SAR data during pretraining, then evaluate on agricultural downstream tasks.
AI.result: On the SICKLE benchmark, the final model achieves 84.9% IoU on crop type mapping, outperforming optical baselines by 15.3 percentage points and existing SAR baselines by 2.2 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SSL pipeline demonstrates that SAR-only pretraining with enhanced temporal pretext tasks (masking and curriculum learning) is highly effective for agricultural monitoring, particularly for crop type mapping, surpassing both optical and existing SAR baselines.

title: PRMU: A Corpus-Free Benchmark for Person-Centric Knowledge Unlearning in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in storing and recalling rich person-related knowledge, raising increasing concerns about reliable knowledge removal. However, existing machine unlearning approaches for MLLMs typically assume access to original forget and retain corpora, which are often unavailable in realistic deletion scenarios. To address this limitation, we introduce PRMU, a benchmark for evaluating corpus-free multimodal unlearning under realistic person-centric deletion requests. PRMU focuses on naturally acquired person-related knowledge and evaluates whether models can remove target knowledge while preserving related knowledge through diverse textual and visual probes, including adversarial evaluation and fine-grained locality analysis. To facilitate research in this setting, we further introduce Similarity-Gated Projection Editing (SGPE), a lightweight corpus-free unlearning baseline with knowledge displacement, protected parameter-space editing, and locality-aware multimodal control. Extensive experiments on representative MLLMs reveal that existing unlearning methods often suffer from unfavorable forgetting-locality trade-offs, with significant locality degradation under aggressive forgetting settings, and remain vulnerable to multimodal knowledge reactivation. Meanwhile, SGPE provides a competitive trade-off between target forgetting, locality preservation, and general multimodal utility. We hope PRMU can facilitate future research toward realistic and scalable multimodal machine unlearning. Code and dataset will be released at https://github.com/2231122/PRMU.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PRMU, a benchmark for corpus-free multimodal unlearning under realistic person-centric deletion requests, along with SGPE, a lightweight corpus-free unlearning baseline. It reveals that existing unlearning methods suffer from forgetting-locality trade-offs and remain vulnerable to multimodal knowledge reactivation, while SGPE offers a competitive balance.
AI.motivation: Existing machine unlearning approaches for MLLMs typically require access to original forget and retain corpora, which are often unavailable in realistic deletion scenarios. The authors aim to address this limitation by evaluating corpus-free multimodal unlearning under realistic person-centric deletion requests.
AI.method: The paper proposes PRMU benchmark focusing on naturally acquired person-related knowledge with diverse textual and visual probes including adversarial evaluation and fine-grained locality analysis. It also introduces Similarity-Gated Projection Editing (SGPE), a lightweight corpus-free unlearning baseline featuring knowledge displacement, protected parameter-space editing, and locality-aware multimodal control.
AI.result: Experiments on representative MLLMs show that existing unlearning methods often suffer from unfavorable forgetting-locality trade-offs with significant locality degradation under aggressive forgetting settings, and remain vulnerable to multimodal knowledge reactivation. SGPE provides a competitive trade-off between target forgetting, locality preservation, and general multimodal utility.
AI.conclusion: The authors hope PRMU facilitates future research toward realistic and scalable multimodal machine unlearning, with code and dataset to be released publicly.

title: CausalSplat: Towards Comprehensive Hierarchical Reasoning in 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has advanced open vocabulary scene understanding, existing methods remain confined to explicit queries. They struggle to interpret implicit intents, complex spatial constraints, and commonsense reasoning required for practical embodied interactions. To address this gap, we introduce the task of reasoning 3D Gaussian segmentation and construct two benchmarks, Causal-LERF and Causal-ScanNet. These benchmarks systematically evaluate commonsense, spatial, affordance, and counterfactual reasoning. Evaluations reveal that current state of the art methods perform poorly on these reasoning challenges. Therefore, we propose CausalSplat, a framework that integrates vision-language models with 3D scene graphs to disentangle explicit structural perception from implicit logical inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CausalSplat achieves state of the art performance on our reasoning benchmarks while showing strong generalizability on standard referring and open vocabulary 3D segmentation tasks. Project Page: https://jiayuding031020.github.io/CausalSplat

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the task of reasoning 3D Gaussian segmentation and proposes CausalSplat, a framework combining vision-language models with 3D scene graphs to handle implicit intents, spatial constraints, and commonsense reasoning that existing 3DGS methods fail to address. Two benchmarks (Causal-LERF and Causal-ScanNet) are constructed to evaluate reasoning capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting methods for open vocabulary scene understanding are limited to explicit queries and cannot handle implicit intents, complex spatial constraints, and commonsense reasoning needed for practical embodied interactions.
AI.method: CausalSplat integrates vision-language models with 3D scene graphs, separating explicit structural perception from implicit logical inference to address reasoning-based 3D segmentation.
AI.result: CausalSplat achieves state-of-the-art performance on the reasoning benchmarks (Causal-LERF and Causal-ScanNet) while demonstrating strong generalizability on standard referring and open vocabulary 3D segmentation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CausalSplat framework effectively bridges the gap between explicit 3D segmentation and implicit reasoning, advancing 3D Gaussian Splatting toward practical embodied interaction scenarios.

title: MultiModal Code-Switching: Interleaving Visual Objects into Language for Explicit Object-Level Alignment
summary: Existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) predominantly rely on image-text pairs for modality alignment pretraining, mapping global image representations to long textual descriptions. However, this image-level alignment suffers from referential ambiguity: models struggle to infer the correspondences between multiple visual objects and textual entities from the global representation, leading to data inefficiency and suboptimal semantic grounding. To address this, we propose MultiModal Code-Switching (MMCS), a novel pretraining paradigm that provides explicit object-level supervision. Inspired by the linguistic phenomenon of code-switching, MMCS interleaves vision and language by replacing textual entities with their corresponding visual objects, enforcing local vision-language grounding. We further develop a scalable data synthesis pipeline to generate a pretraining dataset of 773K samples with accurate object-entity correspondences. Experiments show that MMCS is highly data-efficient: with only 50K samples, it matches or surpasses models trained on 600K image-text pairs. Furthermore, MMCS consistently improves visual grounding and perception capabilities across varying model scales.

AI.tldr: MMCS is a novel pretraining paradigm for Multimodal LLMs that replaces textual entities with corresponding visual objects (inspired by linguistic code-switching) to provide explicit object-level supervision, overcoming the referential ambiguity of image-level alignment. With only 50K samples, it matches or surpasses models trained on 600K image-text pairs, and consistently improves visual grounding and perception across model scales.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs rely on image-text pairs for modality alignment pretraining, but image-level alignment suffers from referential ambiguity—models struggle to infer correspondences between multiple visual objects and textual entities from global image representations, leading to data inefficiency and suboptimal semantic grounding.
AI.method: The paper proposes MultiModal Code-Switching (MMCS), a pretraining paradigm inspired by the linguistic phenomenon of code-switching, which interleaves vision and language by replacing textual entities with their corresponding visual objects to enforce local vision-language grounding. A scalable data synthesis pipeline generates 773K pretraining samples with accurate object-entity correspondences.
AI.result: MMCS is highly data-efficient: with only 50K samples it matches or surpasses models trained on 600K image-text pairs, and consistently improves visual grounding and perception capabilities across varying model scales.
AI.conclusion: Providing explicit object-level supervision through interleaved vision-language pretraining (MMCS) effectively resolves referential ambiguity and yields significant gains in data efficiency and visual grounding, outperforming traditional image-level alignment approaches.

title: Test-Time Self-Evolving GUI Visual Grounding via Reflection-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: GUI Visual Grounding is a fundamental capability for GUI agents. Existing models typically freeze their parameters after deployment, limiting their ability to adapt to unseen interfaces. Although recent methods attempt to adapt models via test-time reinforcement learning, they cannot reflect upon failed exploration. To overcome this, we propose a Test-Time Self-Evolving framework that enables models to improve after deployment without human-annotated ground truth. It constructs a closed-loop of Exploration, Evaluation, Reflection, and Internalization. Specifically, the agent first explores unseen interfaces by predicting grounding coordinates for given instructions. To evaluate these explorations, we introduce an MLLM-based Reflector to assess the generated results and provide the corresponding reasoning reflections. To internalize reflection knowledge into the model weights, we propose Reflection-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation, which translates high-level reasoning into dense token-level supervision via a conditioned self-teacher. Furthermore, we design a Contrastive Calibration method to prevent incorrect auto-regressive prefixes from corrupting the supervisory signals during failed explorations. Extensive experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate our framework's effectiveness, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 7.4% over the base model. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to successfully exploit on-policy self-distillation for test-time adaptation in GUI visual grounding. By filling the gap in post-deployment adaptation, our framework completes the self-evolving capability of GUI agents. The code will be released.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Test-Time Self-Evolving (TSE) framework for GUI visual grounding that enables GUI agents to adapt to unseen interfaces after deployment without human-annotated labels. It builds a closed loop of Exploration, Evaluation, Reflection, and Internalization, using an MLLM-based Reflector for evaluation, Reflection-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation for weight updates, and Contrastive Calibration to prevent corrupted supervision from failed explorations. The framework achieves 7.4% average accuracy improvement across six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI visual grounding models freeze their parameters after deployment, which limits their ability to adapt to unseen interfaces. Although recent methods attempt test-time adaptation via reinforcement learning, they cannot reflect upon failed exploration, leaving a gap in post-deployment self-improvement for GUI agents.
AI.method: The framework constructs a closed-loop of (1) Exploration: the agent predicts grounding coordinates for unseen interfaces; (2) Evaluation: an MLLM-based Reflector assesses results and provides reasoning feedback; (3) Reflection: high-level reasoning is translated into token-level supervision via Reflection-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation using a conditioned self-teacher; (4) Internalization: a Contrastive Calibration method prevents incorrect auto-regressive prefixes from corrupting supervisory signals during failed explorations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate effectiveness, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 7.4% over the base model. This is the first work to successfully exploit on-policy self-distillation for test-time adaptation in GUI visual grounding.
AI.conclusion: The framework fills the gap in post-deployment adaptation, completing the self-evolving capability of GUI agents. Code will be released.

title: VidForensics-M1: Meta-Detection Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Temporal Grounding for AI-Generated Video Forensics
summary: Recent advances in video generation models have significantly improved the realism of synthetic videos, blurring the boundary between generated and authentic content and raising concerns about misinformation. Existing MLLM-based detectors mainly rely on supervised fine-tuning or label-level reinforcement learning, where coarse supervision limits generalization to unseen scenarios and emerging video generators. To overcome these limitations, we are the first to introduce \textbf{meta-detection} into AI-generated video detection, enabling reliable forgery detection by jointly optimizing predicted labels and supporting evidence within reinforcement learning. This paradigm requires reliable evidence signals and effective mechanisms to integrate them into label-level optimization. Textual rationales provide semantic descriptions of forgery artifacts, but their generation and verification depend on external models, making supervision vulnerable to hallucinations and semantic biases. In contrast, temporal grounding provides more objective and verifiable evidence, as manipulated intervals can be precisely controlled during forgery construction. Based on this insight, we propose an automated data construction pipeline that generates paired real-fake videos by replacing temporal segments with boundary-frame-conditioned video generation models. Furthermore, we introduce \textbf{Evidence-Guided Reward Redistribution}, which performs evidence-aware credit assignment by redistributing rewards among label-correct responses according to evidence quality. This preserves reliable label supervision while encouraging detectors to acquire fine-grained and verifiable forgery localization capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \textbf{VidForensics-M1} effectively leverages verifiable temporal evidence to achieve robust and generalizable AI-generated video detection.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VidForensics-M1, the first meta-detection framework for AI-generated video detection that jointly optimizes predicted labels and temporal evidence within reinforcement learning, using an automated data pipeline with boundary-frame-conditioned video generation and Evidence-Guided Reward Redistribution to achieve robust and generalizable forgery detection.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based video forgery detectors rely on supervised fine-tuning or label-level reinforcement learning with coarse supervision, which limits generalization to unseen scenarios and emerging video generators. The authors propose meta-detection as a novel paradigm to overcome these limitations by jointly optimizing labels and supporting evidence.
AI.method: (1) Introduce meta-detection into AI-generated video detection via reinforcement learning; (2) use temporal grounding as verifiable evidence rather than textual rationales to avoid hallucination and semantic bias; (3) build an automated data construction pipeline that generates paired real-fake videos by replacing temporal segments with boundary-frame-conditioned video generation models; (4) propose Evidence-Guided Reward Redistribution for evidence-aware credit assignment to preserve reliable label supervision while encouraging fine-grained forgery localization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that VidForensics-M1 effectively leverages verifiable temporal evidence to achieve robust and generalizable AI-generated video detection, outperforming approaches that rely on coarse label-level supervision.
AI.conclusion: Temporal grounding serves as more objective and verifiable evidence than textual rationales for forgery detection, and the proposed evidence-guided reward redistribution enables reliable and generalizable AI-generated video detection through meta-detection.

title: Capturing Uncertainty in Human Motion for Representation Learning in Soccer
summary: This paper presents a self-supervised representation learning framework for understanding 3D skeleton-based human motion in soccer, using future motion prediction as the learning objective. Since human motion is inherently uncertain, accounting for multiple plausible futures is essential for capturing the underlying motion dynamics and learning effective representations. To this end, we introduce a conditioning module for motion prediction that models a probabilistic distribution over discretized future motions in 3D Euclidean space, learning multimodality with explicit supervision from future trajectories. Experiments on large-scale soccer player tracking data show that our approach substantially improves motion prediction accuracy. Moreover, the learned representations effectively transfer to multiple soccer downstream applications, demonstrating strong cross-task generalization.

AI.tldr: A self-supervised learning framework for 3D skeleton-based soccer motion that uses future motion prediction with a conditioning module to model multiple plausible futures via probabilistic discretized distributions, improving prediction accuracy and enabling transferable representations.
AI.motivation: Human motion is inherently uncertain with multiple plausible futures, so accounting for multimodality is essential for capturing underlying motion dynamics and learning effective representations in soccer.
AI.method: Future motion prediction as a self-supervised objective, with a conditioning module that models a probabilistic distribution over discretized future motions in 3D Euclidean space, learning multimodality with explicit supervision from future trajectories.
AI.result: Substantially improves motion prediction accuracy on large-scale soccer player tracking data, and learned representations transfer effectively to multiple soccer downstream applications with strong cross-task generalization.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised learning via multimodal future motion prediction yields both better prediction accuracy and broadly transferable representations for soccer-specific tasks.

title: AdvFD: Boosting Visual Generation via Adversarial Fr'echet Distance Loss
summary: Fréchet distance has recently emerged as an effective distribution-level objective for generator post-training, complementing the conventional sample-level diffusion and flow-matching losses. However, directly optimizing Fréchet objectives can cause Fréchet hacking. The target metrics keep improving, but visual quality and Fréchet alignment in other feature spaces may stagnate or deteriorate. We attribute this failure to the static pretrained feature spaces used by existing Fréchet losses. These feature spaces provide incomplete and fixed views of the differences between real and generated distributions. To address this limitation, we propose Adversarial Fréchet Distance (AdvFD), which complements the static representation targets in FD-Loss with a calibrated adversarially learned representation. AdvFD augments the original static Fréchet objective with a learnable representation that adversarially maximizes the Fréchet discrepancy between real and generated samples, while the generator minimizes the same discrepancy in the resulting adaptive feature space. To prevent the adversarial representation from trivially increasing the objective through feature amplification, we further introduce real-feature whitening, which normalizes its scale and covariance geometry and stabilizes the min--max optimization. Extensive experiments show that AdvFD consistently improves one-step generator post-training across both JiT and pMF backbones and across different model scales.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Adversarial Fréchet Distance (AdvFD), a method that complements static Fréchet loss with a calibrated adversarially learned representation to prevent Fréchet hacking during generator post-training, improving one-step generator performance across multiple backbones and scales.
AI.motivation: Fréchet distance is effective for generator post-training but directly optimizing Fréchet objectives can cause Fréchet hacking, where target metrics improve but visual quality and Fréchet alignment in other feature spaces stagnate or deteriorate. This failure is attributed to static pretrained feature spaces providing incomplete and fixed views of real and generated distribution differences.
AI.method: AdvFD augments the original static Fréchet objective with a learnable representation that adversarially maximizes the Fréchet discrepancy between real and generated samples, while the generator minimizes the same discrepancy in the adaptive feature space. A real-feature whitening technique normalizes scale and covariance geometry to prevent the adversarial representation from trivially increasing the objective through feature amplification.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that AdvFD consistently improves one-step generator post-training across both JiT and pMF backbones and across different model scales, mitigating Fréchet hacking and improving visual quality and alignment.
AI.conclusion: Static feature spaces are insufficient for Fréchet-based post-training; incorporating an adversarially learned, calibrated adaptive representation with whitening stabilization effectively prevents Fréchet hacking and improves generator post-training performance.
